_____________________________ 

Appeal from the Circuit Court for Charlotte County. 
Geoffrey H. Gentile, Judge. 

October 23, 2026 

BROWNLEE, J. 

Appellant Robert Dwayne Harris appeals a final judgment of foreclosure, the 
denial of rehearing from that judgment, and the denial of his motion to enjoin the 
foreclosure sale. Appellee Nationstar Mortgage, LLC, concedes the judgment was 
entered without adequate notice to Appellant and that remand for a new foreclosure 
trial is required. 
“A judgment procured without notice or opportunity to be heard is void.” 
Daley v. Elevate Roofing & Exteriors, Inc., 432 So. 3d 653, 656 (Fla. 6th DCA 2026) 
2 

(citing Curbelo v. Ullman , 571 So. 2d 443, 445 (Fla. 1990)). “Notice to legally 
interested parties so that they can assert their claims is the essence of the procedural 
due process protections provided by the Florida Constitution.” Wyrick v. Wyrick, 51 
Fla. L. Weekly D1849, D1850 (Fla. 6th DCA Sept. 2, 2026) (quoting In re Adoption 
of a Minor Child, 593 So. 2d 185, 189 (Fla. 1991)). Here, Nationstar concedes that, 
although Appellant was served with the foreclosure complaint and filed pleadings in 
response, he did not receive notice of the foreclosure trial until after the trial 
occurred. This deprived Appellant of an opportunity to be heard on his defenses to 
the f oreclosure. Appellant brought this to the attention of the trial court on two 
occasions, including in a motion for rehearing, but the court denied that motion, on 
the merits, in an unelaborated order. 
We now accept Nationstar’s concession of error, reverse to vacate the 
foreclosure judgment, and remand for further proceedings. Our disposition makes it 
unnecessary to address Appellant’s arguments concerning the court’s entry of 
judgment without ruling on his motion to dismiss, his arguments on the merits of his 
defenses, or his arguments surrounding the denial of rehearing. See, e.g., Waterfront 
in Naples Condo. Ass’n v. Reynolds Ventures, Inc., 51 Fla. L. Weekly D1728, D1729 
(Fla. 6th DCA Aug. 21, 2026) (“We therefore address only the dispositive issue and 
remand for a trial on the merits.”); see also O’Hair v. O’Hair , 396 So. 3d 630, 634 
(Fla. 6th DCA 2024) (citing Akers v. City of Miami Beach, 745 So. 2d 532, 532 (Fla. 
3 

3d DCA 1999), for the proposition that “appellate courts ‘should not ordinarily 
decide issues not ruled on by the trial court in the first instance’”). 
As to the denial of Appellant’s motion to enjoin the foreclosure sale, we affirm 
because the motion became moot before it was heard, by virtue of the sale taking 
place. See Dolgencorp, Inc. v. Winn- Dixie Stores, Inc., 2 So. 3d 325, 327– 28 (Fla. 
4th DCA 2008) (“Generally, injunctive relief is available to prevent a threatened 
harm but is not available to redress harm which has already occurred.” (quoting 
Speer v. Evangelisto, 662 So. 2d 1340, 1341–42 (Fla. 2d DCA 1995))). Even so, our 
reversal of the foreclosure judgment provides grounds for the parties to seek an order 
in the lower court vacating the foreclosure sale. See Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.540(b)(5). 
Accordingly, we affirm the denial of injunctive relief but reverse the final 
judgment of foreclosure and remand for further proceedings consistent with this 
opinion. 
AFFIRMED in part; REVERSED in part; and REMANDED. 
TRAVER, C.J., and NARDELLA, J., concur. 

Robert Dwayne Harris, Punta Gorda, pro se. 

Zachary Ullman, of Aldridge | Pite, LLP, Delray Beach, for Appellee. 

NOT FINAL UNTIL TIME EXPIRES TO FILE MOTION FOR REHEARING 
AND DISPOSITION THEREOF IF TIMELY FILED

leads.caseName: Thomas Williams v. Creekside Huron Shores LLC
leads.text:
If this opinion indicates that it is “FOR PUBLICATION,” it is subject to 
revision until final publication in the Michigan Appeals Reports. 

-1- 
S T A T E O F M I C H I G A N 

C O U R T O F A P P E A L S 

THOMAS WILLIAMS, 

 Plaintiff-Appellant, 

UNPUBLISHED 
October 22, 2026 
8:55 AM 
v No. 375121 
Sanilac Circuit Court 
CREEKSIDE HURON SHORES, LLC, and 
CREEKSIDE COMMUNITIES, LLC, 

LC No. 23-040295-NO 
 Defendants-Appellees. 

Before: PATEL, P.J., and M. J. KELLY and GARRETT, JJ. 

PER CURIAM. 
 Plaintiff, Thomas Williams, fell on three occasions while walking from his vehicle to his 
manufactured home located on a lot he leased from defendant Creekside Huron Shores, LLC 
(Huron Shores). He filed this action against Huron Shores and defendant Creekside Communities, 
LLC (Creekside), the company that Huron Shores retained to maintain its property , alleging 
common-law negligence and violation of MCL 554.139 and MCL 125.536. Williams appeals by 
right the trial court’s order granting summary disposition in favor of Huron Shores and Creekside. 
He also challenges the trial court’s order denying his motion for reconsideration. Because genuine 
issues of material fact exist regarding Williams’s common-law negligence claims, we reverse the 
trial court’s orders in part and remand for further proceedings. 
I. FACTUAL BACKGROUND 
 Williams lived in a manufactured home on a lot he leased from Huron Shores in its 
manufactured housing community. The lot included a walkway that led from the community 
sidewalk to Williams ’s home situated on the lot. The walkway abutted the sidewalk in a “T” 
formation. The walkway was not level with the community sidewalk, which Williams asserted 
had sunk below the level of the walkway, creating a trip hazard. According to Williams, the 
sidewalk had sunk before he moved onto the lot. Williams estimated the height differential 
between the sidewalk and walkway to be approximately two inches on one side of the walkway 
and one inch on the other side. 
-2- 
Williams’s first fall occurred on June 21, 2023. He went to the store to buy groceries and 
tripped on the raised walkway after he returned and attempted to carry the groceries to his home. 
He fell to the ground and treated his injuries with ice and heat that night. The following day, he 
drove himself to the hospital because he was in severe pain when he awoke. He was advised to 
follow up with his doctors. Williams tripped on the raised edge of the walkway a second time on 
July 17, 2023. He fell to the ground and landed on his right wrist. Four days later, he tripped and 
fell a third time because of the same condition. 
 Williams filed a complaint against Huron Shores. Thereafter, he filed an amended 
complaint adding as a defendant Creekside, the maintenance company Huron Shores hired to 
maintain the manufactured housing community. Williams asserted negligence claims against both 
defendants. He alleged that Huron Shores failed to maintain the sidewalk in a careful and prudent 
manner, contrary to MCL 554.139, MCL 125.536, and the common law . Against Creekside, 
Williams alleged that it failed to maintain the community sidewalks in a reasonable and 
nonnegligent manner in accordance with its contract with Huron Shores. 
 Defendants moved for summary disposition, arguing that MCL 125.536 was inapplicable 
because it applied to dwellings, and Williams ’s falls did not occur in a dwelling. Defendants 
maintained that MCL 554.139 was also inapplicable because Williams ’s one -year lease had 
expired by the time he fell , and he remained on the premises as a month -to-month tenant. 
Defendants asserted that, as stated in the lease agreement, Williams assumed the responsibilities 
set forth in MCL 554.139 after expiration of the lease, including maintaining and repairing the 
intersection of the sidewalk and walkway. Regarding Williams’s common-law claims, defendants 
asserted that the height differential between the sidewalk and walkway was less than one inch as 
established by their expert, Dr. Justin Waxman, and photos that Williams took after he fell. 
Defendants argued that the duty to repair the sidewalk should not be greater than that of 
municipalities “which are clearly more funded.” They maintained that, under MCL 691.1402a, a 
municipality is entitled to governmental immunity if a height differential is less than two inches, 
and Williams has not established a vertical discontinuity of two inches or more. 
 Williams did not respond to defendants ’ motion, which the trial court granted after 
dispensing with oral argument. The court determined that MCL 125.536 was inapplicable because 
it does not apply to private dwellings in a city, village, or township with a population less than 
100,000. Regarding MCL 554.139, the court noted that Williams failed to specify in his amended 
complaint whether he alleged violation of MCL 554.139(1)(a) or (b). The court determined that 
MCL 554.139(1)(b) was inapplicable because that section does not apply to sidewalks located in 
common areas. The court also determined that the sidewalk was not unfit for its intended use as 
stated in MCL 554.139(1)(a) because the purpose of a sidewalk is for walking on it and providing 
access to the areas connected to it. The court noted that “[t]he statute does not require a lessor to 
maintain a sidewalk in ideal condition or in the most accessible condition possible, but merely 
requires the lessor to maintain the sidewalk in a condition that renders it fit for use as a sidewalk.” 
The court concluded that the vertical height discontinuity was approximately 1.4 inches and did 
not render the sidewalk unfit for its intended use. The court also reasoned that Williams had failed 
to respond to defendants’ motion and provide documentary evidence establishing a genuine issue 
for trial as required under MCR 2.116(G)(4). 
 The trial court next addressed Williams’s common-law negligence claims, stating: 
-3- 
 The Defendants argue that the Plaintiff cannot show a breach of a duty owed 
to him as an invitee. Furthermore, the Defendants argue that a private landowner 
should not be held to a higher standard than a municipality for purposes of a vertical 
height discontinuity (less than 1.5” in this case vs. 2.0” for a municipality) related 
to a sidewalk. MCL 600.1402a. The Defendants’ arguments —especially those 
related to MCL 600.1402a—are persuasive to this Court. 
Further, the court again recognized that Williams had failed to respond to defendants’ motion. The 
court therefore granted the motion under MCR 2.116(C)(10) and dismissed Williams’s claims with 
prejudice. 
 Williams moved for reconsideration. He argued that he failed to respond to defendants’ 
motion for summary disposition because he erroneously believed the hearing on the motion had 
been adjourned. Substantively, he conceded that MCL 125.536 and MCL 554.139 (1)(b) were 
inapplicable but argued that defendants failed to maintain the sidewalk in a condition fit for its 
intended purpose as set forth in MCL 554.139(1)(a). He maintained that the height differential 
was a factual issue because his photos indicated a difference of approximately two inches , which 
was greater than the height differential asserted by Dr. Waxman. Williams denied that the lease 
agreement delegated to him, as a holdover tenant, the duty to keep his premises in reasonable 
repair, but asserted that even if it did, he fell because of a problem with the community sidewalk 
in the common area and not because of a condition on his premises. Regarding his common-law 
claims, Williams asserted that the two -inch rule applicable to municipalities did not apply to 
private landowners. 
 The trial court denied the motion. The court noted that it did not enter the order granting 
defendants’ motion for summary disposition until after Williams’s response to the motion was due, 
but Williams failed to file a response. The court indicated that it then decided the matter based on 
the evidence that had been presented and based in part on Williams’s failure to respond to 
defendants’ motion. The court stated that Williams did not seek reconsideration of the court’s 
decision but instead wished to respond to defendants’ motion “through the use of a motion for 
reconsideration.” Accordingly, the court denied Williams’s motion. This appeal followed. 
II. STANDARDS OF REVIEW 
 We review de novo a trial court’s decision on a motion for summary disposition. Houston 
v Mint Group, LLC, 335 Mich App 545, 557; 968 NW2d 9 (2021). When deciding a motion under 
MCR 2.116(C)(10), the trial court must consider the affidavits, deposition testimony, and other 
documentary evidence that the parties submit. Anderson v Transdev Servs, Inc , 341 Mich App 
501, 506; 991 NW2d 230 (2022). Summary disposition is appropriate if the evidence, viewed in 
the light most favorable to the nonmoving party, establishes that there is no genuine issue of 
material fact for trial. Id. at 507. “A genuine issue of material fact exists when the record, giving 
the benefit of reasonable doubt to the opposing party, leaves open an issue upon which reasonable 
minds might differ. ” Id. (quotation marks and citation omitted). We review for an abuse of 
discretion a trial court’s decision on a motion for reconsideration . Farm Bureau Ins Co v TNT 
Equip, Inc, 328 Mich App 667, 672; 939 NW2d 738 (2019). “A trial court abuses its discretion if 
it chooses an outcome outside the range of principled outcomes.” Id. 
-4- 
III. ANALYSIS 
A. MCL 554.139(1)(a) 
 Williams argues the trial court erred by determining that no material factual dispute exists 
regarding whether Huron Shores failed to maintain the sidewalk in a condition that rendered it fit 
for its intended use under MCL 554.139(1)(a). “MCL 554.139 provides a specific protection to 
lessees and licensees of residential property in addition to any protection provided by the common 
law.” Allison v AEW Capital Mgt, LLP, 481 Mich 419, 425; 751 NW2d 8 (2008). “The statutory 
protection under MCL 554.139(1) arises from the existence of a residential lease and consequently 
becomes a statutorily mandated term of such lease.”1 Id. MCL 554.139 states, in relevant part: 
(1) In every lease or license of residential premises, the lessor or licensor covenants: 
(a) That the premises and all common areas are fit for the use intended by the 
parties. 
Our Supreme Court has recognized that a “common area” is “ ‘the portion of demised premises 
used in common by tenants over which landlord retains control ( e.g. hallways, stairs) and hence 
for whose condition he is liable, as contrasted with areas of which tenant has exclusive 
possession.’ ” Allison, 481 Mich at 427 , quoting Black’s Law Dictionary (6 th ed), p 275. The 
parties do not dispute that the sidewalk at issue in this case was a common area. 
 Under MCL 554.139(1)(a), a lessor has a duty to maintain a common area in a condition 
“ ‘fit for the use intended by the parties.’ ” Id. at 429, quoting MCL 554.139(1)(a). “The statute 
does not require any level of fitness beyond what is necessary to allow tenants to use the [common 
area] as the parties intended.” Id. at 431. The statute also does not require a lessor to maintain a 
common area “in an ideal condition .” Id. at 430. “[T]he appropriate inquiry under MCL 
554.139(1)(a) remains whether the common area in question is fit (i.e., adapted, suited, or 
appropriate) for the use intended by the parties. ” Bowerman v Red Oak Mgt Co, Inc , ___ Mich 
___ ; ___ NW3d ___ (2026) (Docket No. 167718); slip op at 18. 
 The parties ostensibly intended the sidewalk at issue to be used for walking and providing 
access to the walkway located on Williams’s lot. The fact that the sidewalk had sunk to a degree, 
creating a height differential between the sidewalk and walkway, d id not render it unfit for this 
use. As the trial court recognized, Williams had used the sidewalk without inci

leads.caseName: Bank of America v. Hambrick
leads.text:
2026 IL App (3d) 250524-U 
No. 3-25-0524 
Order filed October 22, 2026 
NOTICE: This order was filed under Illinois Supreme Court Rule 23 and is not 
precedential except in the limited circumstances allowed under Rule 23(e)(1). 

IN THE 
APPELLATE COURT OF ILLINOIS 
THIRD DISTRICT 

BANK OF AMERICA, N.A., Plaintiff-Appellee, 
v. 
EDWARD HAMBRICK, Defendant-Appellant 
Appeal from the Circuit Court of Will County. 
Honorable Jeffrey J. Tuminello, Judge, Presiding. 
No. 25-SC-2908 

JUSTICE DA VENPORT delivered the judgment of the court. 
Justices Holdridge and Anderson concurred in the judgment. 
ORDER 
¶ 1 Held: The circuit court properly denied defendant’s petition for relief from judgment. The 
court did not err when it denied defendant’s request for a nunc pro tunc correction 
of the record. Defendant forfeited his claims that his constitutional rights to due 
process and free access to the courts were violated. Affirmed. 

¶ 2 Plaintiff, Bank of America, N.A., sued defendant, Edward Hambrick, to recover an unpaid 
credit card balance. The circuit court entered a default judgment in plaintiff’s favor, and it later 
denied defendant’s petition to vacate the judgment under section 2- 1401 of the Code of Civil 
Procedure (Code) (735 ILCS 5/2-1401 (West 2024)). 

- 2 - 
¶ 3 Defendant appeals, contending the circuit court abused its discretion in denying his petition 
and erroneously denied his request for a nunc pro tunc “correction of the record.” He also contends 
the circuit clerk violated his constitutional rights to due process and free access to the courts. We 
affirm. 
¶ 4 I. BACKGROUND 
¶ 5 A. Prejudgment Proceedings 
¶ 6 In April 2025, plaintiff filed a small claims action against defendant, alleging defendant 
had failed to pay a $2,592.43 balance that was due on his credit card account. The circuit clerk, at 
plaintiff’s request, issued a summons with a return date of June 13, 2025, the same day. 
¶ 7 Defendant was served with the summons and complaint on May 3, 2025. Later that month, 
he mailed the circuit clerk two documents titled (1) “non-negotiable notice of acceptance and 
request for performance from accommodation parties [sureties] ‘Andrea Lynn Chasteen’ ‘et al.’ ”; 
and (2) “non-negotiable notice and demand for cross-claim against attorney for plaintiff ‘et al.’ ”
1 
The “non-negotiable notice of acceptance” was file-stamped on May 27, 2025. In both documents, 
defendant stated he was “here by special appearance.” 
¶ 8 On June 13, 2025, the parties appeared before the circuit court. Defendant identified 
himself and stated he was “appearing today by special appearance, not general appearance” and 
that he “reserve[d] all [his] rights under UCC 1-308 without prejudice.” Defendant asked the court 
to “close the account” and discharge the matter. The court ordered defendant to file an appearance 
by July 11, 2025, and continued the matter to July 29, 2025, for a bench trial. The court tendered 
a copy of the order to defendant and warned him that the failure to file an appearance as ordered 

1The titles of these documents, as well as other documents defendant submitted throughout these 
proceedings, were typed in all caps typeface. We have reproduced them in lowercase typeface to aid 
readability. 

- 3 - 
would likely result in a default judgment on the trial date. Defendant did not file an appearance as 
ordered. 
¶ 9 On July 11, 2025, plaintiff moved for a default judgment, which was scheduled for 
presentment on July 21, 2025. Plaintiff sent notice of the hearing to defendant. 
¶ 10 Thereafter, defendant mailed the circuit clerk a “special and limited appearance objecting 
to jurisdiction,” an accompanying memorandum, and several other documents. The documents 
were dated July 11, 2026, and file-stamped on July 16, 2025. In his “special appearance” mailing, 
defendant asserted the court lacked both subject-matter and personal jurisdiction. Defendant also 
stated he did not tender any filing fees with his submission, “as payment would constitute a 
voluntary submission to jurisdiction.” 
¶ 11 On July 21, 2025, plaintiff presented its motion for default judgment. Defendant did not 
appear. The court continued the matter to July 29, 2025, for a hearing on the motion, directing 
plaintiff to give notice of the order to defendant. The next day, plaintiff sent notice as directed. 
¶ 12 On July 28, 2025, plaintiff filed a new motion for default judgment, noting defendant had 
not filed his appearance as of July 22, 2025.
2 Plaintiff included an alternative request for dismissal 
without prejudice because the witness who could substantiate the complaint’s allegations had been 
“assigned to cover other legal matters” for plaintiff. 
¶ 13 On July 29, 2025, the matter was called for trial and a hearing on plaintiff’s default motion. 
Plaintiff appeared, and defendant did not. Accordingly, no trial was held, and the court entered a 
default judgment against defendant, awarding plaintiff $2,592.43 plus $384.96 in costs. 
¶ 14 B. Postjudgment Proceedings 

2Plaintiff filed a notice of hearing on July 22, 2025, stating that its new default motion would be 
presented on July 29, 2025. The motion file-stamped until July 28, 2025. 

- 4 - 
¶ 15 On August 28, 2025, defendant used the court’s electronic filing system for the first time. 
He filed an appearance, signed “without prejudice,” along with a fee-waiver application. The court 
granted the fee waiver. 
¶ 16 On September 18, 2025, defendant electronically filed a “Motion to Vacate Default 
Judgment.” He stated his motion was brought under section 2-1301(e) of the Code (735 ILCS 5/2-
1301(e) (West 2024)) and, “in the alternative,” section 2- 1401 of the Code (735 ILCS 5/2 -1401 
(West 2024)). 
¶ 17 In the section 2-1401 portion of his motion, defendant seemingly asserted the court lacked 
jurisdiction over him. He also stated, without alleging any specific facts, as follows: 
“Plaintiff’s counsel acted as a debt collector and is subject to the Fair Debt Collection 
Practices Act ([‘]FDCPA[’]) [citation]. Their conduct—including misrepresentation of the 
amount and character of the debt, initiated suit in an improper venue, and using unfair 
litigation p ractices—violated [sections] 807, 808, and 811 of the FDCPA. The U.S. 
Supreme Court in Heintz v. Jenkins, 514 U.S. 291 (2005), confirmed that attorneys engaged 
in debt collection are bound by the FDCPA. These violations provide an independent 
meritorious defense and further justify vacating the default judgment.” 
Defendant did not address his failure to appear at the July 11, 2025, hearing on plaintiff’s motion 
for default or his failure to appear on the July 29, 2025, trial date. 
¶ 18 As part of his petition, defendant also requested a “nunc pro tunc order to correct the docket 
and record so that it reflects the true and accurate history of [his] filings.” Defendant listed several 
documents that he had mailed to the circuit clerk but were not filed or that were filed but he 
believed were stamped with an incorrect date. Defendant attached the documents, proof that he 

- 5 - 
had mailed the documents, and correspondence from the circuit clerk stating the reason some of 
the documents were being returned to him without being filed. These included the following: 
(1) his May 2025 mailing with a May, 27, 2025, file stamp ( supra ¶ 7), which, according 
to a return receipt, was actually received by the clerk on May 23, 2025; 
(2) a “non-negotiable notice of special appearance demanding dismissal of plaintiff’s suit 
with prejudice for failure to state a claim for which relief may be granted and notice for 
cross-claim against attorney for plaintiff for cause”, mailed on June 4, 2025; 
(3) a “non-negotiable notice of acceptance,” mailed on June 4, 2025; 
(4) a “notice of inquiry to the clerk of court respecting failure to file form 1066 and form 
1120 to account for taxes mandated to be paid on qualified mortgages and foreclosed 
property acquired by real estate mortgage investment conduits on ‘startup day,’ ” mailed 
on June 4, 2025; 
(5) his July 2025 mailings, file -stamped on July 16, 2025 ( supra ¶ 10), which “were 
returned without docket entry”; 
(6) a “notice to the clerk of court for record correction,” mailed on August 15, 2025, and 
returned to defendant on August 27, 2025; 
(7) a “special and limited appearance in equity only” and “notice of motion to vacate 
default judgment” (combined into one document), mailed on August 15, 2025, and returned 
to defendant on August 27, 2025; and 
(8) a “notice of fault and dishonor,” mailed on August 15, 2025, and returned to defendant 
on August 27, 2025. 
¶ 19 At the hearing on the motion to vacate, the parties’ arguments initially focused on whether 
section 2-1301 was applicable, as defendant’s motion was filed on September 18, 2025, more than 

- 6 - 
30 days after the default judgment was entered. Defendant asserted he had previously submitted a 
motion to vacate within 30 days of the default judgment, which was rejected by the clerk. Neither 
plaintiff nor defendant raised any argument with respect to the section 2- 1401 portion of 
defendant’s motion. 
¶ 20 The court denied the motion, and this appeal followed. 
¶ 21 II. ANALYSIS 
¶ 22 Preliminarily, we note that while the “Motion to Vacate Default Judgment” requested relief 
under sections 2-1301(e) and 2-1401 of the Code, defendant raises no section 2-1301(e) argument 
on appeal. We therefore limit our analysis to whether the court properly denied the section 2-1401 
portion of defendant’s motion. Relatedly, because proceedings under section 2- 1401 are initiated 
by the filing of a petition (see 735 ILCS 5/2- 1401(a) (West 2024)), we will refer to defendant’s 
“motion” as a petition throughout our analysis. 
¶ 23 A. The Court Properly Denied Defendant’s Section 2-1401 Petition 
¶ 24 Defendant first contends the circuit court abused its discretion when it denied his section 
2-1401 petition. Section 2-1401 of the Code allows a party to petition the court to vacate a final 
judgment more than 30 days old. 735 ILCS 5/2-1401 (West 2024). When seeking relief under this 
section, the party must set forth specific factual allegations establishing (1) the existence of a 
meritorious defense or claim, (2) due diligence in presenting the defense or claim to the circuit 
court in the original action, and (3) due diligence in filing the petition. Warren County Soil and 
Water Conservation District v. Walters, 2015 IL 117783, ¶ 51. “The quantum of proof necessary 
to sustain a section 2- 1401 petition is a preponderance of the evidence.” Id. When, as here, a 
defendant raises a fact-based challenge in a 2-1401 petition, we review the court’s decision for an 
abuse of discretion. Id. 

- 7 - 
¶ 25 Defendant’s petition failed to set forth any specific factual allegations to support the 
existence of a meritorious defense. In his petition, defendant asserted he had meritorious defenses 
under sections 807, 808, and 811 of the Federal Debt Collection Practices Act (15 U.S.C. §§ 1692e, 
1692f, 1692i). Even assuming defendant’s purported meritorious defenses under the Fair Debt 
Collection Practices Act “would defeat *** plaintiff’s claim in the underlying action” (Erickson v. 
Mitrione, 2025 IL App (4th) 250297, ¶ 23 (internal quotation marks omitted)), defendant’s petition 
failed to set forth any specific facts to establish those defenses. Indeed, defendant failed to state 
any facts establishing that plaintiff used false, deceptive, or misleading representations in 
connection with collecting the debt (id. § 1692e); used unfair or unconscionable means to collect 
or attempt to collect the debt (id. § 1692f); or brought the action in an improper venue (id. § 1692i). 
¶ 26 Moreover, defendant’s petition failed to set forth any facts to establish he acted diligently 
in the original action. “Due diligence requires the section 2 -1401 petitioner to have a reasonable 
e

leads.caseName: Davis v. Fresno Unified School Dist.
leads.text:
Filed 10/22/26

 CERTIFIED FOR PUBLICATION

 IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA

 FIFTH APPELLATE DISTRICT

STEVEN K. DAVIS,
 F089619
 Plaintiff and Appellant,
 (Super. Ct. No. 12CECG03718)
 v.

FRESNO UNIFIED SCHOOL DISTRICT et al.,
 OPINION
 Defendants and Respondents.

 APPEAL from a judgment of the Superior Court of Fresno County. Jeffrey Y.
Hamilton, Jr., Judge.
 Carlin Law Group and Kevin R. Carlin for Plaintiff and Appellant.
 Reed Smith, Raymond A. Cardozo, Kathryn M. Bayes; Whitney Thompson &
Jeffcoach, Timothy L. Thompson, Mandy L. Jeffcoach; Baker Manock & Jenson, Jerry
H. Mann; Kahn, Soares & Conway and Richard C. Conway for Defendant and
Respondent Harris Construction Co., Inc.
 Creede-Blyth Law and Mark L. Creede for Defendant and Respondent Fresno
Unified School District.
 -ooOoo-
 Plaintiff Stephen K. Davis sued defendants Fresno Unified School District (Fresno
Unified or District) and Harris Construction Co., Inc. (Contractor), alleging defendants’
2012 lease-leaseback agreements for the construction of a $36 million middle school
 violated California’s competitive bidding statutes and conflict of interest laws.
Defendants argued the competitive bidding requirements did not apply because the
project qualified for the exception in Education Code section 17406 (section 17406). In
an earlier 2015 appeal, we concluded section 17406’s exception applied to lease-
leaseback agreements only if the agreements (1) were genuine leases, (2) included “a
financing component for the construction of the project,” and (3) provided for the school
district’s “use of the newly built facilities ‘during the term of the lease.’ ” (Davis v.
Fresno Unified School Dist. (2015) 237 Cal.App.4th 261, 271, review denied, Aug. 26,
2015, S227786 (Davis I).) Applying this interpretation, we concluded Davis had
adequately alleged section 17406’s exception did not apply and, thus, he had stated a
claim for a violation of the competitive bidding statutes. (Davis I, supra, at p. 271.)
 A court trial was held in 2024 on Davis’s competitive bidding and conflict of
interest claims. In its statement of decision, the trial court applied the interpretation of
section 17406 set forth in Davis I1 and determined the lease-leaseback agreement fell
within the exception because the leases were genuine, the construction costs carried by
Contractor provided Fresno Unified with a form of financing, and the new facilities were
used during the term of the lease. Thus, the court concluded Davis had failed to prove a
violation of the competitive bidding statutes. The court also determined Davis had failed
to prove that, as a result of entering into preconstruction services agreements with Fresno
Unified, Contractor was a “officer” or “employee” of Fresno Unified subject to the
conflict of interest prohibition in Government Code section 1090 (section 1090).
Consequently, the court denied the conflict of interest claim. Davis filed this appeal.

1 As explained in part III.C. below, the Davis I interpretation applies in this appeal
pursuant to the doctrine of law of the case, not the conflicting statutory interpretation
adopted in decisions of other districts of the Court of Appeal. In Davis v. Fresno Unified
School Dist. (2023) 14 Cal.5th 671 (Davis III), the Supreme Court stated, “that split of
authority is not before us.” (Id. at p. 684.)

 2.
  First, we conclude the conflict of interest claim was properly rejected. Davis has
not demonstrated the trial court misapplied the legal standards used to determine when an
outside advisor like Contractor is an “officer” or “employee” for purposes of section
1090. Second, we find as a matter of law that the lease-leaseback arrangement did not
qualify for the exception to competitive bidding in section 17406 because the project was
financed by the issuance of bonds, not by Contractor-financing. Third, the remedy for
the competitive bidding violation is set forth in subdivision (d)(1) of section 17406,
which was enacted in 2016 after the decision in Davis I was final. That provision states a
contractor may be paid its reasonable cost of construction, excluding profit, under
agreements that failed to qualify for section 17406’s exception. We conclude the
allowance of the contractor’s reasonable cost of construction is not an unconstitutional
gift. (Cal. Const., art. XVI, § 16.) We also conclude Davis has not shown the trial court
abused its discretion or committed legal or factual error when it included overhead costs
as part of the reasonable cost of the services provided. Based on the court’s finding that
Contractor’s net profit on the project was $236,129, that is the amount Contractor must
refund to Fresno Unified.
 We therefore reverse the judgment and direct the trial court to enter a modified
judgment requiring Contractor to disgorge its profit.
 FACTS
 Sometime around 2006 through 2008, Fresno Unified initiated preparation of a
facilities master plan—that is, a long-range plan for its facilities that included a needs
assessment evaluating the suitability of its schools for student’s educational needs. The
plan was created by an outside firm. It identified major deficiencies throughout the
district and the kinds of projects needed to correct the deficiencies. The Board of
Education of Fresno Unified (board) approved the facilities master plan in 2009. The
facilities master plan also identified areas where new construction was needed.

 3.
  A major need was a middle school in southwest Fresno. Since 1978, southwest
Fresno had no middle school and students from that neighborhood were transported by
bus to four middle schools in other parts of Fresno. The construction of the southwest
middle school—later named the Rutherford B. Gaston Sr. Middle School (Gaston
Project)—was an important part of the facilities master plan.
Bonds
 In March 2001, voters within the school district approved General Obligations
Bond Measure K authorizing Fresno Unified to sell $199 million in bonds to fund the
acquisition, construction, maintenance, and renovation of school facilities. In November
2010, after the board approved the facilities master plan, voters approved General
Obligation Bond Measure Q authorizing Fresno Unified to sell $280 million in bonds to
fund the acquisition, construction, maintenance, and renovation of school facilities. Both
measures authorized an ad valorem tax on taxable property within the school district to
fund Fresno Unified’s payment obligations under the bonds.
Board Communications—Project Delivery Methods
 In December 2010 and January 2011, after the approval of Measure Q, Fresno
Unified’s Deputy Superintendent Ruth F. Quinto prepared, and Superintendent Michael
H. Hanson approved and signed, a series of “board communications” to the members of
Fresno Unified’s Board of Education (board) providing information about the methods
for completing facilities projects. Quinto testified that, as soon as the bond measure
passed, the superintendent wanted to begin educating board members about how Fresno
Unified could most effectively provide for the construction of its school projects and,
thus, avoid surprises as Fresno Unified moved forward with different construction
delivery methods.
 The first of these board communications, “BC No. A.1,” included as attachments
two chapters from the Association of California Construction Managers (ACCM) Project
Delivery Handbook titled “What is Construction Management?” and “What is Agency

 4.
 Construction Management?” The board communication described future topics as
“Project Delivery Overview” and the three basic project delivery methods or models: (1)
traditional design-bid-build, (2) construction manager at risk, and (3) lease-leaseback.
 Subsequent board communications addressed the three delivery methods and
provided chapters from the ACCM handbook describing each method. The three-page
chapter addressing the lease-leaseback method stated it involved the selection of a
developer-contractor to develop a new building or improvements on property the district
owned, followed by the simultaneous execution of “a Site Lease of the property giving
the [developer-contractor] the right to develop the project and a Facilities Lease giving it
the obligation to develop the project and to lease the improvements and the site back to
the District, with the District owning the improvements when the lease expires.” The
description also stated that different school districts and their attorneys had taken
different approaches to financing (if any), selection of the developer-contractor, lease
terms, and the methods for selecting trade contractors. It asserted this flexibility was a
primary attraction of the lease-leaseback method. Next, the description stated:

 “Preconstruction work by the Developer-Contractor up to the time of
 signing of leases is sometimes conducted under a Preliminary
 Services Agreement, although some attorneys draft leases that are
 signed immediately and then amended as design and pricing are
 developed.

 “Some attorneys draft leases providing for pre-construction services,
 even design responsibility, with language that calls for an
 amendment to give approval for construction to proceed including
 setting the date of completion and the Guaranteed Maximum Price.”
 The ACCM handbook’s description stated that “close coordination with a law firm
is critical” due to political sensitivities, the preparation of two additional contracts (i.e.,
the lease and leaseback), and the “decisions about the extent or terms of any financing
required.” In addition, it stated: “An attorney’s advice is also necessary to decide

 5.
 whether a Validation process is advisable. This is a legal proceeding recommended by
some attorneys to obtain court approval of the terms of the lease.”2
Request for Qualifications
 After informing the board about the lease-leaseback delivery method, Fresno
Unified’s next step was to identify construction firms capable of completing school
facilities projects using that delivery method. In March 2011, Fresno Unified published a
request for qualifications3 titled “RFQ No. 110327, Lease Leaseback Services” in the
Fresno Bee newspaper and sent fax transmissions to various third parties. RFQ No.
110327’s introduction stated Fresno Unified was “requesting ‘statements of
qualifications’ from business entities experienced in the Lease Leaseback (LLB) public
project delivery method, or business entities that can demonstrate their competence and
ability to complete a public works project using the lease-leaseback delivery method.”
The request stated Fresno Unified would evaluate and qualify the firms that best met the
District’s needs for future projects based on 16 listed factors and other considerations it
deemed relevant. The factors included “expertise in finance and funding issues” and
experience, expertise, and knowledge of the lease-leaseback process.
 RFQ No. 110327 split the description of the anticipated scope of services into two
categories: (1) assisting with project planning services and (2) construction and post-

2 An overview of validation actions by public agencies and reverse validation
actions is set forth in part I.C. of Davis v. Fresno Unified School Dist. (2020) 57
Cal.App.5th 911, 927–929 (Davis II). California has over 200 statutes, mostly in the
Government Code and Water Code, that authorize validation proceedings. (Davis II,
supra, at p. 929.) The statute at issue in Davis II and Davis III was Government Code
section 53511, which authorizes local agencies to bring an action to determine the
validity of its bonds, warrants, contracts, or obligations or evidence of indebtedness
pursuant to the validation provisions in the Code of Civil Procedure.
3 A request for qualifications asks for information about how the responding firm is
qualified to provide the requested services, which is more general than a request for
proposals regarding a particular project.

 6.

leads.text:
Filed 10/22/26 Joseph F. Farivar Investment Group v. HPC Vineburn CA2/1 
NOT TO BE PUBLISHED IN THE OFFICIAL REPORTS 

California Rules of Court, rule 8.1115(a), prohibits courts and parties from citing or relying on opinions 
not certified for publication or ordered published, except as specified by rule 8.1115(b). This opinion 
has not been certified for publication or ordered published for purposes of rule 8.1115. 

IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA 

SECOND APPELLATE DISTRICT 

DIVISION ONE 

JOSEPH F. FARIVAR INVESTMENT 
GROUP, INC., et al., 

 Plaintiff and Respondents, 

 v. 

HPC VINEBURN, LLC, et al., 

 Defendants and Appellants. 

 B343432 

 (Los Angeles County 
 Super. Ct. No. 23STCV00319) 

APPEAL from a judgment of the Superior Court of 
Los Angeles County, Rolf M. Treu, Judge. Reversed. 
Goodkin Law Group, Daniel L. Goodkin and Michael A. 
Shakouri for Defendant and Appellant Meruelo Maddux 
Properties-1919 Vineburn Street, LLC. 
Edgcomb Law Group, Tiffany Hedgpeth, John Edgcomb, 
Gabriel J. Padilla and Ferdeza Zekiri for Defendant and 
Appellant HPC Vineburn, LLC. 
Elkins Kalt Weintraub Reuben Gartside, Kenneth A. 
Ehrlich and Sean A. McCormick for Plaintiffs and Respondents. 

 2 
This case concerns the passive1 migration of contaminated 
groundwater from one property to an adjacent downgradient 
property. Plaintiffs are the owner and renter of the 
downgradient property. The defendants are the current and 
prior owners of the upgradient property. Prior to defendants’ 
ownership, a manufacturing company contaminated the 
upgradient property, and the contamination migrated onto the 
downgradient property. 
The trial court granted summary adjudication in favor of 
plaintiffs on their causes of action for declaratory relief, 
negligence, continuing nuisance, and continuing trespass. After 
plaintiffs dismissed their remaining causes of action, the trial 
court entered judgment in favor of plaintiffs in the amount of 
$12,245,108.42. The judgment included a declaration that 
defendants were responsible for the 1,4-dioxane contamination in 
the groundwater on plaintiffs’ property. 
We conclude plaintiffs failed to show breach of a common 
law or statutory duty of care as a matter of law to support their 
negligence claim. We also conclude plaintiffs did not establish, as 
a matter of law, all elements of their continuing nuisance and 
continuing trespass claims because they used an improper 
damages measure for these continuing torts. Additionally, we 
conclude that the trial court erroneously partially summarily 
adjudicated the declaratory relief cause of action. The trial court 
thus erred in summarily adjudicating plaintiffs’ claims and 
ultimately entering judgment in plaintiffs’ favor. Accordingly, we 
reverse. 

1 Plaintiffs do not allege the defendants themselves caused 
toxic chemicals to enter the groundwater on the upgradient 
property. 

 3 
BACKGROUND 
The record is prolix. We summarize below the overall 
procedural and factual background, and in our Discussion, post, 
we provide additional factual background pertaining to certain 
appellate challenges, 
1. The parties 
Plaintiff Joseph F. Farivar Investment Group, Inc. 
(Farivar) owns property located at 4335 Valley Boulevard 
(Farivar Property). Plaintiff Bordan Shoe Company, Inc. 
(Bordan) leases the Farivar Property. The Los Angeles Regional 
Water Quality Control Board (LARWQCB) issued a cleanup and 
abatement order for the Former Square D Site, which is located 
on the Farivar Property.2 The Square D site began remediation 
efforts in 2000, which efforts continued through 2022. 
The Farivar Property is located adjacent to property at 
1919 Vineburn Avenue (Vineburn Property) and is 
“downgradient” from the 1919 Vineburn Property. Defendant 
HPC Vineburn LLC (Vineburn) currently owns the 
1919 Vineburn Property, which defendant Meruelo Maddux 
Properties-1919 Vineburn Street, LLC (Maddux) previously 
owned. Prior to Maddux’s ownership, the Nardon Manufacturing 
Company owned the Vineburn Property. 

2 Plaintiffs’ expert, Steven Luis, references this cleanup 
and abatement order in his report. The order is not in our record. 

 4 
2. Undisputed facts3 
Prior to 1989, the Nardon Manufacturing Company, a 
metal fabricator, operated the Nardon Facility at the Vineburn 
Property. The Nardon Manufacturing Company discharged 
waste onto the property, including 1,4-dioxane, a common 
additive to 1,1,1-trichloroethene (1,1,1-TCA). 1,4-dioxane, 1,1-
dichloroethene (1,1-DCE), and tetrachloroethylene (PCE) are 
present in the soil and groundwater at the Vineburn Property. 
In 2018, the LARWQCB issued a directive to Vineburn to 
“complete site assessment activities to further assess possible 
source areas that might be present and possibly contributing to 
the groundwater issues and contamination of the Farivar 
Property.” To comply with this directive, Vineburn retained 
Hazard Management Consulting, Inc. (HMC) to conduct a 
subsurface investigation and prepare a report. HMC prepared its 
report dated May 7, 2020. 
HMC’s report, which is central to the issues in this case, 
showed that soil and groundwater contamination at the Vineburn 
Property had migrated to the subsurface of the Farivar Property. 
Vineburn and plaintiffs agree, “The 2020 Subsurface Report 
revealed ‘elevated concentrations of 1,4-dioxane, 1,1-DCE, PCE, 
and to a lesser extent, TCE . . . in soil samples collected’ from a 
boring adjacent to and downgradient from a former wastewater 
clarifier at the northeast end of the Nardon Facility.” “The 2020 

3 Plaintiffs and Vineburn agreed on many facts in their 
separate statements. Maddux did not file a separate statement 
or opposing memorandum of points and authorities. The 
“undisputed facts” referenced in this Background are facts agreed 
to by Vineburn and plaintiffs in their respective separate 
statements. 

 5 
Subsurface Report revealed that ‘laboratory results of 
groundwater samples indicated elevated concentrations of 1,4-
dioxane, 1,1-DCA, and PCE, and to a lesser extent, 1,1-DCA, 1,2-
DCA, and TCE’ at the Nardon Facility.” “There is a ‘hot-spot’ of 
contamination ‘in the vicinity’ of a former wastewater clarifier at 
the northeast end of the Nardon Facility.” “A ‘hot-spot’ is ‘an 
area with much higher concentrations when compared to 
surrounding sample points.’ ” According to the Subsurface 
Report, the Vineburn Property “ ‘has contributed to the 1,4-
dioxane groundwater issues at [the Farivar Property], and to a 
lesser extent the residual 1,1-DCE and PCE at that property.’ ” 
After receiving HMC’s report, Vineburn made a “ ‘proposal 
to start cleaning-up the impacted ground water’ identified by the 
2020 Subsurface Report.” Vineburn is “ ‘ready to start the clean-
up with all the money set aside to do the clean-up’ of the 
contamination revealed by the 2020 Subsurface Report.” 
On September 27, 2023, after plaintiffs filed the case before 
us, the LARWQCB sent Vineburn an order for additional 
investigation of the contamination. The order required Vineburn 
to submit by December 25, 2023 a “work plan . . . to complete the 
vertical and lateral delineation of soil, soil vapor, and 
groundwater impacts.” The LARWQCB noted that HMC’s 2020 
report suggested “a release point in the vicinity of the Former 
Clarifier” at the Nardon Facility, and that the Nardon Facility 
“has contributed to the 1,4-dioxane groundwater plume at the 
downgradient Former Square D Facility [located on the Farivar 
Property], and to a lesser extent the residual 1,1-DCE and PCE 
at that same site.” 

 6 
3. First amended complaint 
Plaintiffs alleged causes of action for continuing nuisance, 
continuing trespass, negligence (including negligence per se), and 
declaratory relief, among other causes of action dismissed after 
the trial court granted summary adjudication in their favor.4 As 
to each cause of action, plaintiffs allege the migration of toxic 
chemicals from Vineburn’s Property to Farivar’s Property. 
Plaintiffs alleged Maddux is a dissolved Delaware limited 
liability company that owned the Nardon Facility from 
approximately 2005 through 2013. Plaintiffs further alleged 
Vineburn has owned and occupied the Nardon Facility since 
2013. Plaintiffs alleged that between 1951 and 1993, the owners 
and occupants of the Nardon Facility manufactured metal 
components and fabricated products for the Los Angeles Metro 
and Standard Light Rail Vehicles. The Nardon Facility’s 
operations included using the solvent, 1,1,1-trichlorethane, which 
is commonly used in connection with 1,4-dioxane. Plaintiffs 
averred the Nardon facility generated hazardous substances that 
were released “into several onsite clarifiers, and subsequently 
disposed of through the municipal sewer system.” 
Contamination from 1,4-dioxane migrated from the Nardon 
Facility to groundwater beneath the Farivar Property. As to the 

4 Plaintiffs also alleged permanent nuisance, permanent 
trespass, contribution, and equitable indemnity. They did not 
seek summary adjudication of these causes of action and later 
dismissed them. 
Plaintiffs also sued the Nardon Liquidating Corp., 
Benedetta Nardon, Marilyn Knoop, and Patricia Minni. These 
defendants are not included in the judgment and are not parties 
to the appeal. 

 7 
continuing nuisance claim, plaintiffs alleged pursuant to Civil 
Code section 3483 that defendants, as successive owners, are 
liable for contamination created by a former owner. They 
incorporated this allegation in their continuing trespass, 
negligence, negligence per se, and declaratory relief causes of 
action. 
In their declaratory relief cause of action, as described in 
more detail in the Discussion, plaintiffs alleged defendants are 
responsible for the contamination and the costs of remediation, 
liabilities to third parties, including governmental agencies, and 
monetary damages. Plaintiffs alleged defendants denied these 
obligations and an actual controversy exists. 
4. Motion for summary adjudication 
Plaintiffs moved for summary adjudication. They relied 
heavily on HMC’s (Vineburn’s consultant) 2020 report, which 
concluded the Vineburn Property “contributed” to the 
contamination at the Farivar Property. 
With respect to damages, plaintiffs relied on declarations of 
their experts, Steven Luis and Bradley Lofgren. Luis, a civil 
engineer with more than 20 years’ experience in environmental 
consulting and engineering services, opined that to clean up the 
1,4-dioxane on the Farivar Property without access to the 
Vineburn Property would cost $11,779,000 (present value) for 
over a 20-year cleanup period. Lofgren, a certified appraiser, 
opined it would cost $192,887 (present value) in loss of use of the 
property during the 20-year remediation. 
In his declaration, Luis stated he was “asked to review 
available environmental information and data related to the 
Former Square D Site [located on the Farivar Property] and 
Former Nardon Site [located on the Vineyard Property] and 

 8 
develop a plan and cost estimate to remediate the contamination 
that has migrated onto the Former Square D Site from the 
Former Nardon Site.” “The Former Square D Site was used 
previously to manufacture electrical components and furniture 
(LARWQCB, 12/5/2001).” Luis recounted a study by Schneider 
Electric, which “attributed the presence of PCE, TCE, 1,1-DCE, 
1,1-DCA, and 1,4-dioxane in groundwater at the Former Square 
D Site to historical releases at the Former Nardon Site due to the 
location of the Former Nardon Site upgradient from the Former 
Square D Site (i.e., the Former Nardon Site is located northeast 
and upgradient of the Former Square D Site . . . .).” Luis also 
described the HMC report’s conclusion that the former Nardon 
Site contributed “ ‘to the 1,4-dioxane groundwater issues’ ” at the 
Former Square D Site. 
Luis referred to a 2023 order from the LARWQCB (the 
order issued afte

leads.caseName: U.S. Bank N.A. v. Sukljian
leads.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York
leads.text:
U.S. Bank N.A. v Sukljian 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06191 
 October 22, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Third Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 U.S. Bank National Association, as Trustee, Respondent, 
 v 
 Moses Sukljian, Appellant, et al., Defendants. 

 Decided and Entered:October 22, 2026 
 CV-25-1318 
 Calendar Date: September 17, 2026 
 Before: Clark, J.P., Ceresia, Mcshan And Powers, JJ. 

 Sandra Poland Demars, Albany, for appellant. 
 Hinshaw & Culbertson LLP, New York City (Claire A. Standish of counsel), for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 Clark, J.P. 
 Appeal from an order of the Supreme Court (Christina Ryba, J.), entered July 24, 2025 in Albany County, which granted plaintiff's motion for, among other things, summary judgment. 
 In December 2005, defendant Moses Sukljian (hereinafter defendant) executed a promissory note in favor of WMC Mortgage Corp., which was secured by a mortgage on real property in Albany County. In 2018, after the note had been transferred to Ocwen Loan Servicing, LLC, FN1 defendant entered into a loan modification agreement with Ocwen that increased the principal balance of the mortgage loan and set forth a new monthly payment amount. 
 On July 17, 2023, plaintiff commenced this mortgage foreclosure action, alleging that it was the holder of the subject note and mortgage and that defendant was in default under the terms of the loan. FN2 Defendant answered and asserted affirmative defenses, including that plaintiff lacked standing to commence the action. Thereafter, plaintiff filed a motion seeking, among other things, summary judgment in its favor, an order dismissing defendant's affirmative defenses, and the appointment of a referee to ascertain and compute the amount due and owing to it. Defendant opposed the motion, arguing, as relevant here, that plaintiff did not sustain its prima facie burden to demonstrate that it was the holder of the note at the time the action was commenced for the purposes of establishing standing, and that there were triable issues of fact precluding judgment as a matter of law in plaintiff's favor. 
 By order entered July 24, 2025, Supreme Court, as relevant here, granted plaintiff's motion for summary judgment, struck defendant's answer, and referred the matter to a referee to ascertain and compute the amount due and owing to plaintiff. In a corresponding written decision, Supreme Court found that plaintiff established its standing to commence the action by demonstrating that it was the holder of the subject note at the time it commenced the action. Additionally, the court held that plaintiff established its entitlement to judgment as a matter of law by submitting "testimonial and documentary evidence showing a valid note and mortgage and defendant's default thereon," and that defendant failed to raise a triable issue of fact in opposition sufficient to defeat such showing. Defendant appeals. 
 In support of its motion for summary judgment, plaintiff submitted a copy of the underlying note, mortgage and loan modification agreement, along with proof of defendant's default, including a copy of defendant's mortgage payment history and a notice that had been sent to defendant reflecting his failure to make required monthly payments. Although such evidence would ordinarily be sufficient to establish plaintiff's entitlement to judgment as a matter of law, because defendant raised the affirmative defense of lack of standing in its answer, plaintiff was also required to prove that it had standing to commence the action in order to be entitled to relief ( see [*2] Bayview Loan Servicing, LLC v Freyer , 192 AD3d 1421, 1422 [3d Dept 2021]; McCormack v Maloney , 160 AD3d 1098, 1099 [3d Dept 2018], lv dismissed 32 NY3d 1185 [2019]; Bank of N.Y. Mellon v Cronin , 151 AD3d 1504, 1506 [3d Dept 2017], lv dismissed 31 NY3d 1061 [2018]; Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Monica , 131 AD3d 737, 738 [3d Dept 2015]). 
 "A plaintiff demonstrates standing in a mortgage foreclosure action by establishing that it is both the holder or assignee of the subject mortgage and the holder or assignee of the underlying note at the time the action is commenced" ( Wilmington Sav. Fund Socy., FSB v LaFrate , 215 AD3d 1023, 1024 [3d Dept 2023] [internal quotation marks and citations omitted]; see U.S. Bank Trust, N.A. v Varian , 156 AD3d 1255, 1256 [3d Dept 2017]). However, "it is not necessary to have possession of the mortgage at the time the action is commenced," as "[a] transfer in full of the [note] obligation automatically transfers the mortgage as well[,] unless the parties agree that the transferor is to retain the mortgage" ( Aurora Loan Servs., LLC v Taylo r, 25 NY3d 355, 361 [2015]). "As such, it is the note, rather than the mortgage, that conveys standing to foreclose" ( Bank of N.Y. Mellon v Cronin , 151 AD3d at 1506 [citations omitted]), and the plaintiff must establish either "[w]ritten assignment of the underlying note or physical delivery of the note sometime prior to the commencement of the [foreclosure] action" ( U.S. Bank N.A. v Shaughnessy , 178 AD3d 1324, 1327 [3d Dept 2019]; see U.S. Bank Trust, N.A. v Varian , 156 AD3d at 1256). "Holder status is established where the plaintiff possesses a note that, on its face or by allonge, contains an [e]ndorsement in blank or bears a special [e]ndorsement payable to the order of the plaintiff" ( Citibank, NA v Abrams , 144 AD3d 1212, 1214-1215 [3d Dept 2016] [internal quotation marks and citation omitted]; see U.S. Bank Trust, N.A. v Varian , 156 AD3d at 1256). 
 Here, plaintiff asserted standing as the holder of the note at the time the action was commenced rather than as the assignee of the note. Although plaintiff attached a copy of the underlying note to the complaint and affirmed therein that it was in possession of the note prior to commencement of the action, the copy of the note attached to the complaint was not endorsed in blank, specially endorsed to plaintiff or accompanied by an allonge containing the required endorsements ( see Residential Mtge. Loan Trust 2013-TT2 v Kaodichimma , 212 AD3d 742, 743 [2d Dept 2023]; McCormack v Maloney , 160 AD3d at 1100). "[W]here there is no allonge or note that is either endorsed in blank or specially endorsed to the plaintiff, mere physical possession of a note at the commencement of a foreclosure action is insufficient to confer standing or to make a plaintiff the lawful holder of a negotiable instrument for the purposes of enforcing the note" ( Fifth Third Bank, N.A. v Stitt , 240 AD3d 576, 577 [2d Dept 2025] [internal quotation marks and citations omitted [*3] ]; see McCormack v Maloney , 160 AD3d at 1100). 
 Plaintiff's evidence in support of its summary judgment motion also did not establish its standing to foreclose the mortgage. In that regard, plaintiff submitted with its motion papers, among other things, a copy of the underlying note and two undated allonges, one of which contained a special endorsement that made the note payable to the order of plaintiff. FN3 However, mere possession of such allonges was insufficient to establish standing without evidence that they were "so firmly affixed" to the note "as to become a part thereof" at the time the action was commenced (UCC § 3-202 [2]; see U.S. Bank N.A. v Chrismas-Beck , 219 AD3d 534, 537 [2d Dept 2023]; U.S. Bank N.A. v Moulton , 179 AD3d 734, 737 [2d Dept 2020]). Plaintiff did not submit any evidence indicating that either allonge was firmly affixed to the note at the time the action was commenced or that it even possessed the allonges at that time ( see U.S. Bank N.A. v Chrismas-Beck , 219 AD3d at 537; U.S. Bank N.A. v Moulton , 179 AD3d at 737). 
 In addition to being undated, the allonges were not attached to or mentioned in the complaint ( compare Flat Rock Mtge. Inv. Trust v Lott , 214 AD3d 1221, 1222 [3d Dept 2023]). Although plaintiff produced an affirmation from a senior loan analyst for PHH Mortgage Corporation — plaintiff's loan servicer/attorney-in-fact — confirming that PHH came into possession of the "original Note" prior to commencement of the action, the senior loan analyst provided no information about whether the note was accompanied by the allonges and, if so, whether the allonges were "firmly affixed" thereto ( compare Aurora Loan Servs., LLC v Taylor , 25 NY3d at 360; U.S. Bank N.A. v Craft , 240 AD3d 1140, 1142 [3d Dept 2025]; LNV Corp. v Allison , 206 AD3d 710, 712 [2d Dept 2022]; Goldman Sachs Mtge. Co. v Mares , 166 AD3d 1126, 1129 [3d Dept 2018]; Citibank, NA v Abrams , 144 AD3d at 1215). The senior loan analyst provided no information about the date of the creation of the allonges or the time frame when plaintiff took possession of the note and allonges. On this record, plaintiff failed to establish as a matter of law that it had standing to commence the action, necessitating reversal of so much of Supreme Court's order as granted summary judgment in plaintiff's favor ( see United Wholesale Mtge., LLC v Smith , 237 AD3d 1339, 1341-1342 [3d Dept 2025]; Citimortgage, Inc. v Ustick , 188 AD3d 793, 795 [2d Dept 2020]; U.S. Bank N.A. v Shaughnessy , 178 AD3d at 1326; Wells Fargo Bank, NA v Ostiguy , 127 AD3d 1375, 1377 [3d Dept 2015]). 
 Ceresia, McShan and Powers, JJ., concur. 
 ORDERED that the order is modified, on the law, without costs, by reversing so much thereof as granted that part of plaintiff's motion as sought summary judgment on the complaint, the appointment of a referee and to strike defendant's answer; motion denied to that extent; and, as so modified, affirmed. 

 Footnotes 

Footnote 1
 In 2019, Ocwen Loan Servicing, LLC merged into PHH Mortgage Corporation, which is the current loan servicer for the subject mortgage and attorney-in-fact to plaintiff. 

Footnote 2
 Plaintiff commenced this action as "U.S. Bank National Association, as Trustee, successor in interest to Bank of America, National Association, as Trustee, successor by merger to LaSalle Bank National Association, as Trustee for Residential Asset Mortgage Products, Inc., Mortgage Asset-Backed Pass-Through Certificates, Series 2007-RP2." 

Footnote 3
 The other allonge was from plaintiff to its wholly owned subsidiary, "U.S. Bank Trust Company, National Association, as Trustee, successor-in-interest to Bank of America[ ] National Association, as Trustee, successor by merger to LaSalle Bank National Association, as Trustee for Residential Asset Mortgage Products, Inc., Mortgage Asset-Backed Pass-Through Certificates, Series 2007-RP2." During the pendency of the action, plaintiff moved to amend the caption of the complaint to substitute the wholly owned subsidiary as the plaintiff. Supreme Court granted the motion in the order on appeal.

leads.caseName: Crocker Park, L.L.C. v. Westlake
leads.text:
[Cite as Crocker Park, L.L.C. v. Westlake, 2026-Ohio-4138.] 

COURT OF APPEALS OF OHIO 

EIGHTH APPELLATE DISTRICT 
COUNTY OF CUYAHOGA 

CROCKER PARK, LLC, ET AL., : 

 Plaintiffs-Appellees, : 
 No. 115356 
 v. : 

CITY OF WESTLAKE, OHIO, : 

 Defendant-Appellant. : 

JOURNAL ENTRY AND OPINION 

 JUDGMENT: AFFIRMED IN PART, REVERSED IN PART, 
 AND REMANDED 
RELEASED AND JOURNALIZED: October 22, 2026 

Civil Appeal from the Cuyahoga County Court of Common Pleas 
Case No. CV-24-106203 

Appearances: 

Benesch, Friedlander, Coplan & Aronoff, LLP, Gregory J. 
Phillips, and Alayna K. Bridgett, for appellees. 

Michael P. Maloney, Westlake Director of Law, and Robin 
R. Leasure, Westlake Assistant Director of Law; Seeley, 
Savidge, Ebert & Gourash Co., LPA and Christopher M. 
Corrigan, for appellant. 

ON RECONSIDERATION1 

EILEEN T. GALLAGHER, P.J.: 

 Defendant-appellant City of Westlake, Ohio (“Westlake” or “the City”) 
appeals two orders granting partial motions for summary judgment against 
Westlake and in favor of plaintiffs-appellees Crocker Park, L.L.C. (“CP”), CP Phase 
I Residential Delaware, L.L.C., Crocker Excelsior, L.L.C., CP Commercial Delaware, 
L.L.C. (“CP Commercial”), and CP Land, L.L.C. (collectively “plaintiffs”) and third-
party-defendant-appellee Crocker Park Management, L.L.C. (“CP Management”). 
Westlake claims the following errors: 
1. The Court of Common Pleas abused its discretion in ordering the 
plaintiffs to file summary judgment when pleadings had not been 
finalized and discovery had not been conducted on the issues[.] 
2. The court erred [in] granting summary judgment when the parties 
had not conducted discovery on the facts of the dispute and all 
information was not before the court[.] 
3. The court erred in granting plaintiffs’ summary judgment on 
defendant’s counterclaim for slander of title[.] 
4. The court erred [in] granting plaintiffs summary judgment on 
defendant’s . . . abuse of process claim[.] 
5. The court erred [in] declaring that plaintiffs have not waived their 
ability/right to assert its right of first refusal on future offers[.] 
 We find that the trial court did not err in granting the parties leave to 
file motions for summary judgment by March 17, 2025, because the pleadings had 

1 The original decision in this appeal, Crocker Park, L.L.C. v. Westlake, 2026-Ohio-
2932 (8th Dist.), released on July 30, 2026, is hereby vacated. This opinion, issued upon 
reconsideration, is the court's journalized decision in this appeal. See App.R. 22(C); see 
also S.Ct.Prac.R. 7.01. 

closed by that time, and Westlake could have sought leave for additional discovery 
pursuant to Civ.R. 56(F), if additional discovery were needed. We further find that 
the trial court properly granted summary judgment in favor of plaintiffs and the 
third-party defendant on Westlake’s slander -of-title and abuse -of-process claims. 
However, because we find that CP failed to properly exercise its right of first refusal 
within a reasonable time, we find that the trial court erred in declaring that CP did 
not waive its right of first refusal. We, therefore, affirm the trial court’s judgment in 
part, reverse it in part, and remand the case to the trial court for further proceedings. 
I. Facts and Procedural History 
 Plaintiffs filed a complaint and a verified amended complaint against 
Westlake, alleging the breach of multiple contracts and seeking various forms of 
declaratory and injunctive relief as well as money damages.2 The allegations arose 
from the parties’ relationship to a mixed-use development located on Crocker Road 
in Westlake, Ohio, known as “Crocker Park.” 
 Crocker Park was developed on multiple contiguous parcels of property 
and contains a mix of retail stores, restaurants, office buildings, apartments, and 
green spaces. The Crocker Park planners intended the different parcels of property 
that compose Crocker Park “to interrelate and function to their mutual advantage 
and benefit such that the eventual owners of the parcels, and their permittees, would 

2 The allegations in, and the exhibits attached to, the amended complaint were 
verified under oath by Steve Coven, the secretary of CP and general counsel of Stark 
Enterprises, Inc., CP’s agent, exclusive property manager, and leasing agent. 

have access to certain ‘common areas’ throughout the development.” (Verified 
amended complaint ¶ 12.) Thus, CP drafted a “Declaration of Covenants, 
Conditions, Restrictions and Easements” (the “Declaration”) governing the use and 
ownership of the various parcels that compose Crocker Park. 3 The Declaration 
identifies CP as the declarant and defines the term “Owner” or “Owners” to mean 
“the current and future owners of the parcels comprising Crocker Park.” (Verified 
amended complaint, Exhibit A.) 
 One of the disputes between plaintiffs and Westlake involved the cost 
of maintaining and repairing “Common Areas.” Section 1.9 of the Declaration 
defines the term “Common Area,” in part, as “all portion of the Project Site available 
for the general use, c onvenience and benefit of all Owners and their respective 
Permittees,” subject to some exceptions not relevant to this case. 
 Section 1.10 of the Declaration defines the term “Common Expenses” 
as follows: 
The term “Common Expenses” means (i ) the cost and expense of 
operating, maintaining, repairing and replacing the Common Area 
and/or the Public Improvements, including, but not limited to, all costs 
and expenses incurred by [CP Management] under the Management 
Agreement; (ii) the cost of utilities serving the Common Areas and/or 
the Public Improvements, (iii) the cost of garbage and trash removal 
for the Project, except special charges that can be specifically identified 
as belonging to one Parcel, (iv) the cost, expense, and premium for all 
insurance attributed to Common Areas; (v) Real Estate Taxes for the 
Common Areas and/or the Public Improvements (if any), and (vi) any 

3 The Declaration was verified and submitted with the verified amended complaint 
as Exhibit A. Coven also verified the authenticity of the Declaration in an affidavit 
submitted with plaintiffs and third -party defendant’s motion for partial summary 
judgment. 

other cost, expense, fee or charge deemed a Common Expense under 
this Declaration. 
 Regarding maintenance and repair of Common Areas, Section 6.2 of the 
Declaration provides: 
Subject to the payment provisions in Section 6.4 hereof and the 
easements, terms, covenants, conditions, restrictions and rights 
granted, declared and/or reserved hereunder, the Common Areas shall 
at all times be maintained and managed by Declarant except that each 
Owner is required to provide security for the Common Areas located 
within its respective Parcel and Declarant shall have the obligation and 
responsibility to keep, maintain, manage and operate the Common 
Areas in good, clean operating condition, order and repair consistent 
with the operation of similar first -class mixed -use developments 
located in the State of Ohio and shall keep the Common Areas clean 
and (as applicable) reasonably clear of snow and ice. Notwithstanding 
the foregoing, Declarant agrees that the Public Improvements, if 
constructed, may be maintained and managed by [CP Management] in 
accordance with standards established under applicable Port Authority 
Agreements. Declarant shall (and [CP Management], as to the Public 
Improvements, may) manage, calculate and coordinate among the 
Owners the payment of Common Expenses. 
 Section 6.4 of the Declaration governs payment of Common Expenses 
and states, in relevant part: “Each Owner shall pay to Declarant (or [CP 
Management] as to the Public Improvements), pursuant to the provisions of this 
Section 6.4, its share of the Common Expenses, calculated based on the Budget and 
such Owner’s Proportionate Share.” Section 1.50 defines the term “Proportionate 
Share” as “the percentage assigned by Declarant from time to time with respect to 
each Parcel/Owner.” (Declaration p. 8.) Section 6.4(b) requires that “[e]ach 
Owner’s share of the Common Expenses shall be paid in equal monthly installments 
in such amounts as are reasonably estimated and billed by Declarant.” The 

Declaration was recorded with the Cuyahoga County Recorder on December 8, 
2003. (Verified amended complaint ¶ 29.) 
 In March 2014, CP and Westlake executed the “Market Square 
Development Agreement” (the “Development Agreement”) whereby CP agreed to 
“convey to the City, at no cost to the City, approximately two (2) acres of land within 
[Crocker Park].”4 (Verified amended complaint ¶ 32; development agreement p. 1.) 
In exchange for the free land, Westlake “agreed to construct on the Parcels, at the 
City’s cost, a market square with improvements to be designed and adjacent open 
space.” (Verified amended complaint ¶ 33; development agreement p. 1.) The land 
conveyed to Westlake, together with its improvements, is known as “Market 
Square.” (Verified amended complaint ¶ 35.) Westlake accepted deeds to the land 
subject to “any reservations, restrictions, limitations, easements, and conditions of 
title[,]” including the conditions of title outlined in the Declaration. (Verified 
amended complaint ¶ 37-38.) Hence, Westlake became an owner of Crocker Park 
subject to the covenants, conditions, and restrictions set forth in the Declaration. 
 Market Square was constructed and became operational in 2015. 
(Verified amended complaint ¶ 47.) It is comprised of an indoor event space, a half-
acre outdoor green space, and two restrooms with entrances on the exterior of the 
building. The restrooms h ave been open to all “Permittees” since they were 

4 The Development Agreement is attached to the verified amended complaint as 
Exhibit B. 

constructed.5 (Verified amended complaint ¶ 49.) Plaintiffs allege that “Market 
Square’s greenspace and restrooms constitute Common Areas as defined in the 
Declaration.” (Verified amended complaint ¶ 50.) They also allege that “Market 
Square’s common restrooms must remain open and accessible to other Owners and 
their Permittees in order for Crocker Park to comply with local zoning and building 
codes.” (Verified amended complaint ¶ 51.) 
 In September 2015, Westlake entered into an Operation and 
Maintenance Agreement (“O&M Agreement”) with CP Management, a wholly 
owned subsidiary of CP.6 Under the O&M Agreement, CP Management agreed to 
operate and manage Market Square. Section 3(b) of the O&M Agreement provides, 
among other things, that CP Management will perform “all maintenance and repairs 
to [Market Square].” The O&M Agreement furth er states that “[i]n the event that 
revenues in any year are insufficient to pay in full all out -of-pocket expenses from 
the operation of [Market Square], [CP Management] will be obligated to pay the 
unpaid portion of such out-of-pocket expenses.” (Verified amended complaint ¶ 57; 
O&M Agreement, Section 3(c).) 
 CP Management operated Market Square for eight years until 
Westlake terminated the agreement in December 2023. Plaintiffs allege there were 
insufficient revenues to pay for out -of-pocket expenses related to the operation of

occupants, including tenants, of the Parcels and their and each Owner’s respective

licensees and concessionaries.” 
6 The O&M Agreement is attached to the original complaint as Exhibit D.

the eight years that CP Management managed Market Square. (Verified amended 
complaint ¶ 60-61.) As a result, CP Management paid the out -of-pocket expenses, 
including Common Expenses, for the eight years it managed Market Square. 
 Plaintiffs allege that after the O&M Agreement terminated on 
December 31, 2023, CP Ma
