 United States Court of Appeals
 for the Federal Circuit
 ______________________

 DEBORAH E. BARRON, JOHN BUENAVENTURA
 BAEZ, JAMES ACHILLE, JONATHAN ACHILLE,
 THE ALB REVOCABLE TRUST, THE RPB
 REVOCABLE TRUST, COURTYARD VILLAS, L.L.C.,
 RONALD NOURSE, OLD FOREST LAKES OWNERS
 ASSOCIATION, GILDA PASCUAL, STEPHEN
 STILLER, CHRISTOPHER WORMWOOD, SHARON
 KRUEGER, JAMES MUSSELWHITE, ENOS
 WEAVER, JR., ANNA MARY WEAVER, WILLIS
 MARTIN, ALTA MARTIN, JAMES MYERS,
 KATHERINE MYERS, JUNE SHUMWAY, DANIEL J.
 MALLON, IRENE A. MALLON, AS TRUSTEES OF
 THE MALLON FAMILY TRUST UNDER
 AGREEMENT DATED OCTOBER 3, 2007,
 Plaintiffs-Appellants

 ALEXANDRINE L. BOSWELL, TRUSTEE OF THE
 ALB REVOCABLE TRUST, DATED JULY 21, 2003,
 ROMAN P. BOSWELL, TRUSTEE OF THE RPB
 REVOCABLE TRUST, DATED AUGUST 31, 2004,
 JACEK GATKIEWICZ, HANNA GATKIEWICZ,
 JONATHAN LESTER, ANAPAULA V. LESTER,
 Plaintiffs

 v.

 UNITED STATES,
 Defendant-Appellee
 ______________________

 2025-1179
 ______________________
 Case: 25-1179 Document: 75 Page: 2 Filed: 10/22/2026

 2 BARRON v. US

 Appeal from the United States Court of Federal Claims
 in No. 1:21-cv-02181-EHM, Judge Edward H. Meyers.

 --------------------------------------------------

 4023 SAWYER ROAD I, LLC, DOUGLAS ABBOTT,
 CYNTHIA G. ABBOTT, JULIA R. ADKINS, AUSTIN
 C. MURPHY, RONALD S. ALBRITTON, JOYCE S.
 ALBRITTON, LOUIS J. ALDERMAN, JR. AS
 TRUSTEE OF LOUIS L. ALDERMAN 2013
 REVOCABLE TRUST, NEAL ATCHLEY, JO
 ATCHLEY, JEFFREY DOYLE,
 Plaintiffs

 JOHN M. ALVIS, ET AL.,
 Plaintiffs-Appellants

 v.

 UNITED STATES,
 Defendant-Appellee
 ______________________

 2025-1459
 ______________________

 Appeal from the United States Court of Federal Claims
 in Nos. 1:19-cv-00757-EHM, Judge Edward H. Meyers.
 ______________________

 Decided: October 22, 2026
 ______________________

 MARK F. HEARNE, II, True North Law Group, LLC, St.
 Louis, MO, argued for plaintiffs-appellants.

 EMILY POLACHEK, Appellate Section, Environment and
 Case: 25-1179 Document: 75 Page: 3 Filed: 10/22/2026

 BARRON v. US 3

 Natural Resources Division, United States Department of
 Justice, Bloomington, MN, argued for defendant-appellee.
 Also represented by ADAM R.F. GUSTAFSON, MARY
 GABRIELLE SPRAGUE, Washington, DC.
 ______________________

 Before LOURIE, STOLL, and STARK, Circuit Judges.
 LOURIE, Circuit Judge.
 This appeal arises from a rails-to-trails land conversion
 in Florida carried out under the National Trails System Act
 Amendments of 1983 (the “Trails Act”). Appellants Debo-
 rah E. Barron et al. (collectively, “Landowners”) own land
 adjacent to a rail corridor on which Seaboard Air Line Rail-
 way (“Seaboard”) historically operated a railroad. In May
 2019, the Surface Transportation Board (“STB”) issued a
 Notice of Interim Trail Use (“NITU”) on a segment of that
 rail corridor. Landowners argued that the NITU issuance
 constituted a taking of their property by the United States
 without the just compensation required by the Fifth
 Amendment.
 In two decisions constituting the appealed orders, the
 Court of Federal Claims (“the Claims Court”) disagreed,
 determining that the railroad owned title to the land in fee
 simple and thus no Fifth Amendment taking occurred.
 Barron v. United States, 174 Fed. Cl. 114, 119 (2024); 4023
 Sawyer Rd. I, LLC v. United States, 175 Fed. Cl. 79, 81
 (2025). Landowners now appeal, arguing that the Claims
 Court erred in its ownership and taking determinations.
 We affirm.
 BACKGROUND
 Railroad operators seeking to abandon a railroad must
 file an application with (or seek an exemption from) the
 STB, which has regulatory authority over railroad lines.
 Caldwell v. United States, 391 F.3d 1226, 1229–30
 (Fed. Cir. 2004) (citing 49 U.S.C. §§ 10903, 10502). But in
 Case: 25-1179 Document: 75 Page: 4 Filed: 10/22/2026

 4 BARRON v. US

 seeking abandonment authority, railroad operators may
 utilize the Trails Act “to convert their rail corridors to trails
 rather than abandon them altogether.” Pressly v. United
 States, 174 F.4th 1368, 1373 (Fed. Cir. 2026) (citing Na-
 tional Trails System Act Amendments, Pub. L. No. 98-11,
 § 208(2), 97 Stat. 42, 48 (1983) (codified at 16 U.S.C.
 § 1247(d))). That involves a “railbanking” process, which
 “allows a railroad to negotiate with a state, municipality,
 or private group (the ‘trail operator’) to assume financial
 and managerial responsibility for operating the railroad
 right-of-way as a recreational trail.” Caldwell, 391 F.3d at
 1229. “If the railroad [and trail] operator[s] agree[] to in-
 terim trail use, STB will issue an NITU.” Pressly,
 174 F.4th at 1373 (citing 49 C.F.R. § 1152.29(d)(1)). An
 NITU allows a railroad to “discontinue service, cancel tar-
 iffs, and salvage track and other equipment” without le-
 gally abandoning the line. Caldwell, 391 F.3d at 1230.
 Critically, when the STB issues an NITU, “state law
 reversionary interests that would otherwise take effect
 pursuant to normal abandonment proceedings are fore-
 stalled,” id. at 1236, which may result in an unconstitu-
 tional Fifth Amendment taking (depending on what, if any,
 reversionary interests there are) unless the property
 holder receives just compensation, Pressly, 174 F.4th at
 1373.
 In the instant case, the land at issue is an approxi-
 mately 7.68-mile segment of a railway line known as the
 Venice Branch. Barron, 174 Fed. Cl. at 119. 1 As relevant
 on appeal, the railroad acquired an interest in the Venice
 Branch from Landowners’ predecessors-in-interest via two

 1 Because the factual background regarding the land
 and railroad line is substantially the same for both Claims
 Court cases from which Landowners appeal, we cite only
 Barron. See Barron, 174 Fed. Cl. at 119; 4023 Sawyer Rd.,
 175 Fed. Cl. at 82–83.
 Case: 25-1179 Document: 75 Page: 5 Filed: 10/22/2026

 BARRON v. US 5

 mechanisms: a set of conveyance deeds––from Sarasota
 Land Company (“SLC”), Clough, Burton, Neihardt, two
 from Florida Mortgage and Investment Company
 (“FMIC”), and Ringling––and the judgment of a 1926 con-
 demnation proceeding (“Condemnation Judgment”). Bar-
 ron, 174 Fed. Cl. at 119; 4023 Sawyer Rd., 175 Fed. Cl. at
 82–83.
 In March 2019, the operator of the corridor, Seminole
 Gulf Railway, L.P., filed a notice of exemption to abandon
 the Venice Branch. Barron, 174 Fed. Cl. at 119. In re-
 sponse, the Sarasota County Board of County Commission-
 ers filed a Request for Public Use Condition and Request
 for Interim Trail Use with the STB. J.A. 185–88. The STB
 then issued an NITU for the Venice Branch under § 8(d) of
 the Trails Act. Barron, 174 Fed. Cl. at 119.
 Landowners then sued the United States in the Claims
 Court, claiming that the deeds and Condemnation Judg-
 ment conveyed to the railroad only an easement in the land
 underlying the Venice Branch, and thus the issuance of the
 NITU prevented what they assert is their fee title from be-
 coming unencumbered upon abandonment, leaving them
 with a reversionary interest and resulting in an unconsti-
 tutional taking. Barron, 174 Fed. Cl. at 119–20; 4023 Saw-
 yer Rd., 175 Fed. Cl. at 82. The government countered that
 the conveyance deeds and Condemnation Judgment con-
 veyed a fee simple interest to the railroad such that no tak-
 ing occurred. Barron, 174 Fed. Cl. at 120; 4023 Sawyer
 Rd., 175 Fed. Cl. at 82.
 The Claims Court agreed with the government. Bar-
 ron, 174 Fed. Cl. at 138–39; 4023 Sawyer Rd., 175 Fed. Cl.
 at 97–98. It first concluded that each deed unambiguously
 conveyed a fee simple interest, relying on the deeds’ broad
 conveyance language, specific mention of the land, and lack
 of any reversionary clause. Barron, 174 Fed. Cl. at 126–
 32; 4023 Sawyer Rd., 175 Fed. Cl. at 91–94. Second, as to
 Case: 25-1179 Document: 75 Page: 6 Filed: 10/22/2026

 6 BARRON v. US

 the Condemnation Judgment, the Claims Court deter-
 mined that the language concerning the type of estate con-
 veyed was ambiguous, but nonetheless concluded, after
 consulting extrinsic materials from the condemnation pro-
 ceeding, that the Condemnation Judgment also conveyed
 to the railroad title in fee simple. Barron, 174 Fed. Cl. at
 132–38.
 Because, in its view, each deed and the Condemnation
 Judgment conveyed title to the railroad in fee simple, the
 Claims Court granted summary judgment to the govern-
 ment. Barron, 174 Fed. Cl. at 138–39; 4023 Sawyer Rd.,
 175 Fed. Cl. at 97–98. Landowners appealed, and we have
 jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(3).
 STANDARD OF REVIEW
 “We review a grant of summary judgment by the Court
 of Federal Claims de novo.” Pressly, 174 F.3d at 1374 (cit-
 ing Barlow v. United States, 86 F.4th 1347, 1353 (Fed. Cir.
 2023)). “Summary judgment is appropriate only where,
 when drawing all reasonable inferences in favor of the non-
 moving party, there are no genuine issues of material fact
 and the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter
 of law.” Id. “Whether a taking has occurred is a question
 of law based on factual underpinnings.” Chi. Coating Co.,
 LLC v. United States, 892 F.3d 1164, 1169 (Fed. Cir. 2018)
 (quoting Stearns Co. v. United States, 396 F.3d 1354, 1357
 (Fed. Cir. 2005)). “We conduct a plenary review of the legal
 conclusions of the [Claims Court] while reviewing its fac-
 tual conclusions for clear error.” Id. (modifications added).
 DISCUSSION
 The instant dispute turns on whether the deeds and
 Condemnation Judgment conveyed an interest in fee sim-
 ple or merely an easement. See Pressly, 174 F.4th at 1373.
 If they conveyed an interest in fee simple, there was no re-
 versionary interest left to the Landowners’ predecessors-
 in-interest, no taking occurred, and we must affirm. Id.
 Case: 25-1179 Document: 75 Page: 7 Filed: 10/22/2026

 BARRON v. US 7

 Conversely, if they conveyed only an easement for railroad
 use, there was a reversionary interest, and we must re-
 verse and remand for the Claims Court to determine the
 nature and status of the easement. See Preseault v. United
 States, 100 F.3d 1525, 1533 (Fed. Cir. 1996) (en banc). But
 first, because “acquisition of property rights is governed by
 the law of the state in which the property sits,” Pressly,
 174 F.4th at 1374, we review relevant Florida law.
 I
 This court and the Claims Court have encountered
 Florida law in rails-to-trails cases before; most relevant
 here is the Rogers line of cases. See, e.g., Rogers v. United
 States, 184 So. 3d 1087 (Fla. 2015) (“Rogers IV”); Rogers v.
 United States, 814 F.3d 1299 (Fed. Cir. 2015) (“Rogers V”).
 There, we certified questions of Florida law to the Florida
 Supreme Court, which the Florida Supreme Court an-
 swered in Rogers IV. See 184 So. 3d at 1100.
 As relevant here, the Florida Supreme Court in Rogers
 IV provided the following guiding principles on Florida law:
 (1) “the effect of a deed, both as to the property conveyed
 and the character of the estate conveyed, is determined by
 the intent of the grantor,” id. at 1095; (2) “[w]hen the lan-
 guage of a deed is clear and certain in meaning and the
 grantor’s intention is reflected by the language employed,
 there is no room for judicial construction of the language
 nor interpretation of the words used,” id. (quotation omit-
 ted); (3) “[w]hen a deed is unambiguous and sufficient on
 its face to show the grantor’s intent as to the property de-
 scribed and the estate conveyed, extrinsic evidence is not
 admissible to vary the terms,” id. at 1100 (citations omit-
 ted); and (4) “the amount of consideration stated in a deed
 provides no basis for questioning the validity of the deed,”
 id. at 1097 (citations omitted).
 Case: 25-1179 Document: 75 Page: 8 Filed: 10/22/2026

 8 BARRON v. US

 II
 With the above guiding principles in mind, we turn
 first to the deeds for each conveyance.
 A
 Each conveyance deed contains explicit language
 granting rights in the land itself without any reversionary

leads.caseName: Daniel Skidmore v. Hideo Hayashi
leads.text:
If this opinion indicates that it is “FOR PUBLICATION,” it is subject to
 revision until final publication in the Michigan Appeals Reports.

 STATE OF MICHIGAN

 COURT OF APPEALS

DANIEL SKIDMORE, FOR PUBLICATION
 October 21, 2026
 Plaintiff-Appellant, 11:44 AM

v No. 371345
 Oakland Circuit Court
HIDEO HAYASHI, MAKIE HAYASHI, and JULIE LC No. 2023-198678-CH
SKIDMORE,

 Defendants-Appellees,

and

POTOMOC TOWNE II ASSOCIATION,

 Defendant.

HIDEO HAYASHI and MAKIE HAYASHI,

 Plaintiffs-Appellees,

v No. 371349
 Oakland Circuit Court
DANIEL SKIDMORE, LC No. 2022-194491-CK

 Defendant-Appellant,

and

JULIE SKIDMORE,

 Defendant.

Before: MURRAY, P.J., and BOONSTRA and RIORDAN, JJ.

 -1-
 BOONSTRA, J.

 These consolidated appeals arise from a landlord-tenant dispute about the habitability of a
rental unit and the tenants’ continued obligation to pay rent. Landlords Hideo and Makie Hayashi
sued defendants Daniel and Julie Skidmore for breach of contract. In a separate lawsuit, Daniel
raised several related claims against the Hayashis, Julie,1 and Potomac Towne II Association (the
Association).2 The trial court consolidated the two cases. In Docket No. 371345, Daniel appeals
by right the trial court’s order granting summary disposition in favor of Julie and the Hayashis on
Daniel’s claims against them. In Docket No. 371349, Daniel also appeals by delayed leave
granted3 the same order granting summary disposition in favor of the Hayashis on their claims
against Daniel. We affirm in part, reverse in part, and remand for further proceedings.

 I. PERTINENT FACTS AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY

 In June 2017, Daniel and Julie entered into a one-year lease agreement with the Hayashis
to rent a condominium unit owned by the Hayashis in Oakland County. In May 2018, the parties
extended the lease through June 2019, and in May 2019, they extended the lease through June
2021.

 According to Daniel, upon moving into the unit in 2017, he noticed that the roof and certain
other parts of the unit were leaking. The parties discussed and exchanged several emails regarding
the leaks, and Daniel expressed his frustration that the Hayashis had not done anything about the
leaks despite knowing about the issue for months. The Association’s summary of work orders for
the unit showed that the Skidmores had submitted multiple work orders, associated with various
third-party contractors, related to leaks in the unit throughout their occupancy, all of which had
been marked as “closed.” According to an e-mail sent by a client-communications specialist from
Kramer Triad Management Group to an individual named “Dean,”4 a representative from Kearns
Brothers, Inc. “did a temporary repair on 5-30-18 and sent a proposal for the permanent fix to the
manager.” Dean forwarded the e-mail to Daniel, noted that the repair was a temporary fix, and
asked Daniel to notify him and the service company if he experienced any more rain-water leakage.

 In September 2019, Daniel e-mailed Dean to report concerns about mold in one of the
bedrooms and asking for the Association to “immediately” repair the leak in the roof and for a
mold inspector to be sent to the unit to assess the damage and give repair recommendations. In
April 2020, Julie e-mailed Dean to report the Skidmores’ concerns about continued leaking, noting

1
 The Hayashis dismissed their complaint against Julie with prejudice. This opinion also addresses
Daniel’s claims against Julie, but Julie has not filed a brief in this appeal.
2
 Daniel settled his claims against Potomac. The trial court accordingly dismissed the claims
against Potomac with prejudice, and Potomac is not involved in this appeal.
3
 Hayashi v Skidmore, unpublished order of the Court of Appeals, entered September 26, 2024
(Docket No. 371349). This Court consolidated the appeals on its own initiative in the same order.
Id.
4
 From context, it appears that “Dean” may be a pseudonym for Hideo.

 -2-
 that they had not received “the timeline as to when the roof might be replaced,” that they “had
issues in the past with health problems related to mold allergies, and that the possibility of water
sitting in the rafters and creating moldy conditions” was “a big worry.” In May 2020, Daniel e-
mailed Hideo to inform him that Daniel was canceling the lease because of “constant roof leaks
and mold,” claiming that the Hayashis’ “failure to provide a watertight residence can allow for
termination of a lease.” Daniel left the unit in November 2020 after depositing several months’
rent into an escrow account.5

 The Hayashis sued the Skidmores in 2022, claiming that the Skidmores had breached the
lease agreement by failing to pay $25,034.88 in rent and late fees as of the date that the lease
expired and that they had failed to maintain the premises in good repair. The trial court denied
Daniel’s motion for leave to file a counterclaim against the Hayashis and Julie because he had not
attached a copy of the proposed counterclaim to the motion. Instead of refiling the motion with
the expected attachment, Daniel filed a separate lawsuit. The trial court consolidated the two cases.

 In resolving several motions for summary disposition, the trial court dismissed each of
Daniel’s 18 claims.6 It also granted summary disposition in favor of the Hayashis on their breach-
of-contract claim, leaving only the issue of damages for trial. These consolidated appeals
followed, and this Court stayed further proceedings in the trial court.7

 II. JURISDICTION

 As a preliminary matter, we address the Hayashis’ challenge to our jurisdiction in these
cases. See Clohset v No Name Corp (On Remand), 302 Mich App 550, 560; 840 NW2d 375 (2013)

5
 According to Daniel and Julie’s daughter, Daniel and Julie had ended their relationship in early
2020 and planned to separate in June 2020, but it is unclear when Julie vacated the unit.
6
 On May 2, 2023, the trial court granted partial summary disposition in favor of the Hayashis,
dismissing Count IV (conversion of property other than the security deposit), Count V (violation
of the Truth in Renting Act (TIRA), MCL 554.631 et seq.), Count VI (violation of the Michigan
Consumer Protection Act, MCL 445.901 et seq.), Count XII (violation of the anti-lockout statute,
MCL 600.2918), Count XIII (personal injury), XIV (violation of the Housing Law of Michigan
(HLM), MCL 125.401 et seq.), and Count XV (intentional infliction of emotional distress). On
June 20, 2023, the trial court granted summary disposition in favor of Julie, dismissing Count XVI
(breach of fiduciary duty), Count XVII (contribution), and Count XVIII (breach of contract). On
March 27, 2024, the trial court denied Daniel’s motion for declaratory judgment that the lease was
illegal and granted the Hayashis’ motion for summary disposition, dismissing Count I (illegal
contract), Count II (disgorgement), Count III (unjust enrichment), Count IV (conversion of the
security deposit), Count VII (breach of contract), Count VIII (silent fraud), Count IX (innocent
misrepresentation), Count X (violation of the Landlord-Tenant Act, MCL 554.601 et seq.), and
Count XI (exemplary damages). In the same opinion, the trial court granted summary disposition
in favor of the Hayashis on their breach-of-contract claim against Daniel.
7
 Hayashi v Skidmore, unpublished order of the Court of Appeals, entered September 26, 2024
(Docket No. 371349).

 -3-
 (explaining that all courts must address challenges to subject-matter jurisdiction). We review this
issue de novo. See Chen v Wayne State Univ, 284 Mich App 172, 191; 771 NW2d 820 (2009).
The Hayashis argue that this Court lacks jurisdiction over the claim of appeal in Docket
No. 371345, which is associated with Daniel’s complaint in lower court case no. 2023-198678-
CH, because the trial court consolidated that case with the Hayashis’ case in lower court case no.
2022-194491-CK, which has not been litigated to a final order. The Hayashis also contend that
this Court lacks jurisdiction in Docket No. 371349 because Daniel’s application for leave to appeal
in that case was untimely. We disagree.

 The Hayashis previously brought motions to dismiss these appeals on the same
jurisdictional grounds, which this Court has already denied. Skidmore v Hayashi, unpublished
order of the Court of Appeals, entered September 26, 2024 (Docket No. 371345); Hayashi v
Skidmore, unpublished order of the Court of Appeals, entered September 26, 2024 (Docket
No. 371349). Daniel’s application for leave to appeal in Docket No. 371349 was filed just 30
seconds after the deadline for filing an application under MCR 7.205(A)(1)(b). At this Court’s
request, Daniel promptly amended his application to include a statement of his reasons for the
delay, and this Court granted his delayed application for leave to appeal under MCR 7.205(4).
Regarding Daniel’s claim of appeal in Docket No. 371345, Daniel had the right to appeal the trial
court’s order dismissing his claims because that order was final with respect to lower court case
no. 2023-198678-CH. See Chen, 284 Mich App at 199 (“Because the cases retained their separate
identities [after consolidation], the time for appeal must be determined by reference to the final
judgment or order for the individual cases.”). Accordingly, this Court has jurisdiction and may
determine the issues on appeal.

 III. CLAIMS BETWEEN DANIEL AND THE HAYASHIS (DOCKET NOS. 371345 &
 371349)

 Daniel challenges the trial court’s decision to dismiss many of his claims against the
Hayashis and to grant the Hayashis’ motion for summary disposition of their own breach-of-
contract claim.8 We address each of Daniel’s arguments in turn.

 A. STANDARDS OF REVIEW

 The trial court granted summary disposition of Daniel’s complaint in favor of the Hayashis
and Julie under MCR 2.116(C)(8) and (10). A trial court’s decision on a motion of summary
disposition is reviewed de novo. BC Tile & Marble Co, Inc v Multi Bldg Co, Inc, 288 Mich App
576, 583; 794 NW2d 76 (2010). Certain portions of the trial court’s opinions do not identify
whether its decision was based on MCR 2.116(C)(8) or (C)(10).9 For issues in which the trial

8
 In Docket No. 371345, Daniel appeals the trial court’s decision to grant summary disposition on
Counts I, II, III, IV, V, VII, XI, XII, XIV, XVII, and XVIII. In Docket No. 371349, Daniel appeals
the trial court’s decision to grant summary disposition on the Hayashis’ breach-of-contract claim.
9
 The trial court clearly granted summary disposition under MCR 2.116(C)(10) for the Hayashis’
breach-of-contract claim and under MCR 2.116(C)(8) for Daniel’s Count V (TIRA), Count XIV

 -4-
 court considered documentary evidence outside of the pleadings, this Court will review the trial
court’s decision under MCR 2.116(C)(10). See BC Tile, 288 Mich App at 582 (“Where the parties
rely on documentary evidence, appellate courts proceed under the standards of review applicable
to a motion made under MCR 2.116(C)(10).”) (quotation marks and citation omitted). Otherwise,
we will review the decisions under MCR 2.116(C)(8).

 MCR 2.116(C)(8) tests the legal sufficiency of the complaint. Bailey v Schaaf, 494 Mich
595, 603; 835 NW2d 413 (2013). The trial court must decide the motion on the basis of the
pleadings alone and it must accept as true all factual allegations supporting the claim. Gorman v
American Honda Motor Co, Inc, 302 Mich App 113, 131; 839 NW2d 223 (2013). A motion under
MCR 2.116(C)(8) “may be granted only when the claim is so clearly unenforceable as a matter of
law that no factual development could possibly justify recovery.” Id. at 131-132.

 “MCR 2.116(C)(10) tests the factual sufficiency of the complaint.” Bernardoni v Saginaw,
499 Mich 470, 472; 886 NW2d 109 (2016). Summary disposition under MCR 2.116(C)(10) is
appropriate when, “[e]xcept as to the amount of damages, there is no genuine issue as to any
material fact, and the moving party is entitled to judgment or partial judgment as a matter of law.

leads.caseName: James Raptoplous v. the City of Detroit
leads.text:
If this opinion indicates that it is “FOR PUBLICATION,” it is subject to 
revision until final publication in the Michigan Appeals Reports. 

-1- 
S T A T E O F M I C H I G A N 

C O U R T O F A P P E A L S 

JAMES RAPTOPLOUS and FACILITY ONE, INC., 

 Plaintiffs-Appellants, 

UNPUBLISHED 
October 21, 2026 
10:45 AM 
v No. 373899 
Wayne Circuit Court 
CITY OF DETROIT and WAYNE COUNTY 
TREASURER, 

LC No. 24-000825-CH 
 Defendants-Appellees. 

Before: MURRAY, P.J., and BOONSTRA and RIORDAN, JJ. 

PER CURIAM. 
 Plaintiffs James Raptoplous and Facility One, Inc, 1 appeal by right the trial court’s order 
granting defendant Wayne County Treasurer’s (WCT) motion for summary disposition under 
MCR 2.116(C)(4), (5), (7), (8), and (10).2 We affirm. 
I. PERTINENT FACTS AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY 
 In November 2007, plaintiff entered into a land contract to purchase a parcel of industrial 
property in Detroit. In January 2008, a memorandum of land contract was recorded with the 

1 Plaintiffs’ counsel purports to represent both Raptoplous and Facility One in this appeal. Facility 
One was included as a plaintiff in the initial complaint, and the City of Detroit argued in its answer 
that Facility One lacked standing to sue. Facility One was removed from plaintiff’s amended 
complaint without explanation, and the proceedings subsequently treated Raptoplous as the only 
plaintiff. Accordingly, the term “plaintiff” as used in this opinion refers only to Raptoplous, as 
Facility One’s interests are not at issue in this appeal. 
2 The order appealed from mistakenly states that the trial court denied defendant’s motion for 
summary disposition, but the order was later amended to state that it granted the motion. The order 
does not explicitly address plaintiff’s claim against the City of Detroit, but granting WCT’s motion 
is necessarily fatal to that claim because it was based on WCT’s transfer of its purported interest 
in the property to the City of Detroit after the foreclosure. 
-2- 
Wayne County Register of Deeds. The memorandum described the property’s street address as 
“19935 Hoover, Detroit, MI” and included its tax parcel identification (tax parcel ID) number and 
its legal description. The seller also conveyed a covenant deed to plaintiff, which included the 
same street address, tax parcel ID, and legal description. The deed was recorded in May 2011. 
Both the deed and the memorandum of land contract listed plaintiff’s address as “46913 Fields 
Drive” in Shelby Township. 
 In 2015, plaintiff became delinquent in his property taxes , and in 2017, WCT initiated an 
action under the General Property Tax Act (GPTA), MCL 211.78 et seq., to foreclose the property. 
WCT conducted a title search for the property in September 2017. WCT’s notice of the show 
cause hearing and the judicial foreclosure hearing stated the correct tax parcel ID and legal 
description for the property, but it erroneously stated that the property’s address was “19825 
Hoover.” WCT filed a Proof of Personal Vi sit indicating that a WCT representative visited the 
property on November 20, 2017 at 1:54 a.m., found it to be an unoccupied or abandoned structure, 
then placed a copy of the notice of show cause hearing and judicial foreclosure hearing in a 
conspicuous manner on the property. The Proof of Personal Visit also stated the correct tax parcel 
ID and legal description but used the incorrect “19825 Hoover” address instead of the correct 
“19935 Hoover” address. WCT’s mail log also stated that the personal visit occurred at “19825 
Hoover.” 
According to the affidavit of WCT’s process server, on November 27 and November 29, 
2017, WCT mailed a copy of the notice for the show cause hearing and judicial foreclosure hearing 
by both certified and first-class mail to plaintiff at both “19935 Hoover St” and “46913 Fields Dr.” 
WCT’s mail log also stated that the notice was delivered to the “46913 Fields Dr” address, but it 
did not indicate whether delivery to the “19935 Hoover St” address was successful . Plaintiff 
denied that notice was ever sent to 19935 Hoover St because the certification number associated 
with that address from WCT’s mail log matched a mailing to “20750 Hoover Rd” in Warren, which 
was returned as “undeliverable.” Plaintiff also denied that notice was ever sent to 46913 Fields 
Dr because the certification number from WCT’s mail log matched the certification number for a 
mailing to a “70290 Laurel Creek” address,3 and that document was delivered to and signed for by 
plaintiff’s ex-wife4 on December 4, 2017. Plaintiff asserted that he had never resided at 70290 
Laurel Creek. WCT explained why a copy of the notice was sent to that address: 
Upon information and belief, the fact that the certified mail notice was delivered to 
[7]0290 Laurel Creek Dr, Macomb, MI is because there was a permanent change 
of address on file with the United States Post Office. The National Change of 

3 The parties and the trial court sometimes referred to this address as “20290 Laurel Creek,” but it 
is clear to this Court that the handwritten address in the delivery record from the United States 
Postal Service is “70290 Laurel Creek.” In any event, t he correct street number for the Laurel 
Creek address is not relevant to this case. 
4 Plaintiff and his ex-wife were divorced in 2013, and plaintiff asserts that they were estranged at 
the time that the notice was delivered to her. 
-3- 
Address (NCOA) database indicated that the change of address was under code “F” 
(Family) and became effective in September of 2017. 
Finally, on December 8 and December 15, 2017, a copy of the notice for the show cause 
hearing and judicial foreclosure hearing was published in the Detroit Legal News, a newspaper 
that circulates in Wayne County. The notice included plaintiff’s name and used “19825 Hoover” 
as the property’s address. 
In March 2018, the trial court entered an uncontested judgment of foreclosure, which was 
subsequently recorded in the register of deeds. The judgment of foreclosure vested title in WCT. 
In October 2018, WCT executed a quitclaim deed conveying its interest in the property to the City 
of Detroit and recorded the transfer. 
Plaintiff became aware of the foreclosure sometime in 2018 and attempted to negotiate 
with the City of Detroit to purchase the property. After years of communication, the negotiations 
fell through, and the City of Detroit initiated eviction proceedings against plaintiff. 
In January 2024, plaintiff initiated an action to quiet title to the property, arguing that 
plaintiff retained fee title to the property because the judgment of foreclosure was invalid. In lieu 
of filing an answer, WCT filed a motion for summary disposition under MCR 2.116(C)(4), (5), 
(7), (8), and (10), arguing, inter alia, that the judgment of foreclosure was valid and could not be 
set aside because WCT had complied with the notice requirements under MCL 211.78i. The City 
of Detroit stated that it “fully concurs” in WCT’s motion and that granting the motion would also 
necessitate dismissing the claims against the City. 
After a hearing, the trial court granted the motion for summary disposition, holding that 
WCT had satisfied the requirements for notice and minimum due process and that plaintiff 
accordingly had no basis to challenge the judgment of foreclosure. Plaintiff moved for 
reconsideration, but the trial court denied the motion. This appeal followed. 
II. SUMMARY DISPOSITION 
 Plaintiff argues that the trial court erred when it granted defendant’s motion for summary 
disposition because WCT failed to comply with statutory and constitutional notice requirements 
during the foreclosure proceedings, which rendered the judgment of foreclosure invalid .5 We 
disagree. 
A. STANDARD OF REVIEW 
 “We review a trial court’s decision on a motion for summary disposition de novo on the 
basis of the entire record to determine if the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of 
law.” Silberstein v Pro -Golf of America, Inc , 278 Mich App 446, 457; 750 NW2d 615 (2008). 

5 Plaintiff raised additional arguments in support of his action to quiet title in the trial court, but 
we do not address those arguments because plaintiff has not raised them on appeal. 
-4- 
The trial court granted WCT’s motion for summary disposition on the basis of MCR 2.116(C)(4), 
(7), (8), and (10). 6 “Where a motion for summary disposition is brought under both 
MCR 2.116(C)(8) and (C)(10), but the parties and the trial court relied on matters outside the 
pleadings, as is the case here, MCR 2.116(C)(10) is the appropriate basis for review.” Silberstein, 
278 Mich App at 457. We must consider “affidavits, pleadings, depositions, admissions, and other 
evidence submitted by the parties in the light most favorable to the party opposing the motion. 
Where the proffered evidence fails to establish a genuine issue regarding any mater ial fact, the 
moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.” Maiden v Rozwood, 461 Mich 109, 120; 
597 NW2d 817 (1999) (citation omitted). 
B. MINIMUM DUE PROCESS 
The former owner of a foreclosed property “shall not bring an action, including an action 
for possession or recovery of the property,” more than two years after the judgment of foreclosure 
becomes effective. MCL 211.78l(1). The trial court’s judgment of foreclosure became effective 
in March 2018, but plaintiff did not initiate the action to quiet title until January 2024. Therefore, 
plaintiff’s action is time -barred under MCL 211.78l(1) unless the judgment of foreclosure is set 
aside. Relief from a judgment of foreclosure is appropriate if the foreclosing governmental unit 
did not provide constitutionally sufficient notice of the proceedings. See In re Ingham Co Treas 
for Foreclosure, 331 Mich App 74, 78; 951 NW2d 85 (2020). 
The GPTA “includes an extensive set of procedures for notice of the steps in the tax sale 
process” that our Supreme Court generally has recognized as “a constitutionally sound procedure 
for sale of property because of nonpayment of taxes.” Smith v Cliffs on the Bay Condominium 
Ass’n, 463 Mich 420, 428; 617 NW2d 536 (2000), overruled in part on other grounds by Jones v 
Flowers, 547 US 220; 126 S Ct 1708; 164 LE 2d 415 (2006). Under MCL 211.78i(7)(c), the 
content of the notice must include, among other information, “[a] legal description or parcel 
number of the property and, if available, the street address of the property.” The parties do not 
dispute that the notices that WCT sent contained a typographical error in which the address was 
incorrectly stated as “19825 Hoover” instead of “19935 Hoover,” although the legal description 
and parcel number were correct. The issue is whether the content of the notice complied with the 
GPTA despite the typographical error. 
 In Smith v Cliffs on the Bay Condominium Ass’n (On Remand), 245 Mich App 73, 75; 626 
NW2d 905 (2001), this Court held that a typographical error in the description of a notice of 
foreclosure proceedings does not render the notice insufficient if, “in the hands of an interested 
party of ordinary intelligence, [the notice] would have served to identify the property at issue with 
reasonable certainty.” Plaintiff argues that this case is distinguishable from Smith because rather 
than a minor error in the description of the property, this case involves an error in the property’s 
street address, which is critical to identifying the property. But the fact that the street address is 
only required to be included in the notice “if available” indicates that it is possible to identify the 
property at issue with just the legal description and parcel number. See MCL 211.78i(7)(c). An 
interested party of ordinary intelligence would have known that he had an interest in a property 

6 The court rejected WCT’s claim under MCR 2.116(C)(5) (lacking legal capacity to sue). That 
decision is not relevant to this appeal. 
-5- 
located

leads.caseName: Trucks Rx Inc v. Padilla Investments LLC
leads.text:
If this opinion indicates that it is “FOR PUBLICATION,” it is subject to 
revision until final publication in the Michigan Appeals Reports. 

-1- 
S T A T E O F M I C H I G A N 

C O U R T O F A P P E A L S 

TRUCKS RX, INC., and MAZEN ABUELEAWAH, 

 Plaintiffs-Appellants, 

and 

JANA TRUCKING LINE, INC., and ALA ABU 
QATTAM, 

 Plaintiffs, 

UNPUBLISHED 
October 21, 2026 
1:51 PM 
v No. 375909 
Wayne Circuit Court 
PADILLA INVESTMENTS, LLC, 

LC No. 24-016734-CB 
 Defendant-Appellee. 

Before: PATEL, P.J., and M. J. KELLY and GARRETT, JJ. 

PER CURIAM. 
 In this landlord -tenant dispute, p laintiffs Trucks Rx, Inc., and Mazen Abueleawah 
(appellants), appeal by right the judgment in favor of defendant, Padilla Investments, LLC, in the 
amount of $411,131.50 against plaintiff Jana Trucking Line, Inc. (Jana Trucking), plaintiff Ala 
Abu Qattam, and appellants .1 On appeal, appellants challenge the arbitration award in favor of 
defendant and the trial court ’s order confirming the award and denying appellants’ motion to 
vacate the award. Because the arbitrator did not exceed his authority or make an error of law in 
rendering his decision, we affirm. 
I. FACTUAL BACKGROUND AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY 

1 Our reference to “plaintiffs” refers to all four plaintiffs, but not all four plaintiffs are appellants. 
Only Trucks Rx and Abueleawah are appellants. Our reference to “tenants” refers to Trucks Rx 
and Jana Trucking only. 
-2- 
 Abueleawah owns Trucks Rx , and Qattam owns Jana Trucking. Alvaro Padilla is the 
managing member and an owner of defendant, which owns the real property at issue in this dispute. 
The property is located in Detroit and was previously used as a hardware store. In February 2022, 
the tenants entered into a three-year commercial lease agreement for the property , which they 
intended to use to sell tires. Abueleawah and Qattam personally guaranteed the lease. The lease 
required the tenants to pay the insurance, utilities, and property taxes on the property and to 
maintain the premises. It specified that the property was to be used for the purpose of selling new 
vehicle tires and for no other purpose without defendant’s written consent. The tenants agreed to 
comply with all laws and ordinances and to assume any financial responsibility required to do so. 
They accepted the property “as is.” 
In February 2022, t he tenants paid the security deposit, took possession of the premises, 
and operated their business. In April 2022, the city of Detroit inspected the property and issued a 
correction order to defendant, which recited several violations of the Detroit Property Maintenance 
Code and/or the city’s zoning ordinance. In June 2022, the city conducted another inspection and 
issued an emergency correction order that again listed several violations, including the illegal use 
of the premises. The city ordered that the present use of the premises be discontinued because no 
permit had been issued for the use. The city also required defendant to correct the deficiencies 
listed and to obtain a certificate of compliance . In July 2022, the tenants stopped paying rent to 
defendant. In August 2022, the city inspected the property and issued another correction order to 
defendant for additional violations, including that the building was “operating illegally as a Major 
Auto Repair/Semi Truck Storage Semi Truck Terminal/Dispatch Office,” when its only legal use 
was retail. In September 2022, the tenants abandoned the premises , and , two months later , 
defendant obtained a certificate of compliance to use the property for a retail or wholesale store. 
The chief problem with the property was that it lacked an automatic sprinkler system , which was 
required to store tires on the property. Padilla offered to accompany Abueleawah to a meeting 
with city officials to help resolve the issue, but Abueleawah did not attend the meeting. Appellants 
estimated the cost of the fire suppression system to be more than $60,000 and to take four to six 
months to install. 
 In October 2022, defendant filed a breach-of-contract action against plaintiffs , and 
plaintiffs counterclaimed against defendant. The parties agreed to resolve the dispute by 
arbitration and dismiss the case. During arbitration, the parties stipulated that the lease contained 
the full agreement between the parties and that the y did not discuss the installation of a fire 
suppression system before signing the lease. The arbitrator determined the tenants breached the 
lease agreement when they stopped paying rent and vacated the premises. He determined that the 
lease was unambiguous, the tenants took the premises “as is,” and they were required to take the 
steps necessary to comply with the laws and regulations to operate their business. The arbitrator 
reasoned “the lease made clear that [defendant] was not required to perform any work with respect 
to” the tenants’ operation of their business on the premises, and the lease instead required the 
tenants to perform the work and to provide defendant with plans and specifications for approval . 
The arbitrator found that Padilla offered to assist the tenants by meeting with city officials, but the 
tenants did not attend the meeting that the city scheduled and never submitted plans and 
specifications to defendant. The arbitrator rejected the plaintiffs’ defense that the lease was void 
or unenforceable and found the caselaw on which they relied distinguishable or inapposite. He 
awarded defendant a total of $411,131.50 plus interest and determined that Qattam and 
Abueleawah were personally liable because they personally guaranteed the tenants’ obligations. 
-3- 
Appellants filed this action, seeking to vacate, modify, or correct the arbitration award. 2 
They alleged the arbitrator exceeded his authority and clearly erred by failing to determine that the 
city’s ordinance required defendant, as the property owner, to obtain a permit to install the 
sprinkler system. They asserted that defendant’s failure to obtain the permit prevented the tenants 
from using the property as contemplated in the lease, which warranted rescission or cancellation 
of the lease. They characterized the sprinkler system requirement as a mutual mistake that would 
have cost the tenants approximately $60,000 and prevented them from operating their business for 
at least four to six months because of the time required to obtain the permit and install the system. 
Defendant moved to confirm the arbitration award, asserting the arbitrator correctly applied 
the law when he interpreted the lease. Defendant asserted that the arbitrator properly rejected the 
argument that defendant was required to obtain the permit and install the sprinkler system because 
the argument was unsupported by the law and undisputed facts of the case. Defendant maintained 
that the lease required the tenants to assume the obligation of complying with all ordinances, and 
the lease was not illegal or unenforceable. Defendant requested the trial court to confirm the 
arbitration award and enter a judgment in its favor. 
The trial court agreed with defendant. The court noted the high standard for overturning 
an arbitrator’s decision and opined that the arbitrator did not legally err by determining that the 
lease imposed on the tenants the obligation to install the sprinkler system. The court stated that 
the arbitrator’s decision was logical and relied on “solid reasoning based upon the plain language 
of the lease which I don’t think is ambiguous.” The court remarked that the decision was perhaps 
“not fair to either side” but noted that the tenants were “in a much better position” than the property 
owner to know whether their business required a sprinkler system to operate. The court denied 
appellants’ motion to vacate the arbitrator ’s award, granted defendant ’s motion to confirm the 
award, and entered a judgment for defendant in the amount of $411,131.50 plus interest . 
Appellants moved for reconsideration, which the court denied. This appeal followed. 
II. ANALYSIS 
A. STANDARDS OF REVIEW AND BASIC LEGAL PRINCIPLES 
 “In civil cases, Michigan follows the raise or waive rule of appellate review.” Tolas Oil & 
Gas Exploration Co v Bach Servs & Mfg, LLC , 347 Mich App 280, 289; 14 NW3d 472 (2023) 
(quotation marks and citation omitted). A party must raise an argument in the trial court and assert 
the same grounds on appeal to preserve the issue for appellate review. Id. This Court is not 
obligated to consider unpreserved issues but “may overlook preservation requirements if the 
failure to consider the issue would result in manifest injustice, if consideration is necessary for a 
proper determination of the case, or if the issue involves a question of law and the facts necessary 
for its resolution have been presented .” Id. at 289 -290 (quotation marks and citations omitted). 
Although appellants failed to preserve the bulk of their arguments for our review, we nevertheless 

2 Although all four plaintiffs were included in the caption of the complaint, the attorney who filed 
the complaint represented appellants only. 
-4- 
address the arguments because they involve questions of law and the facts necessary to resolve the 
arguments have been presented. 
 “This Court reviews de novo a circuit court ’s decision whether to vacate an arbitration 
award.” TSP Servs, Inc v Nat ’l-Std, LLC, 329 Mich App 615, 619 -620; 944 NW2d 148 (2019). 
De novo review “means that we review the legal issues presented without extending any deference 
to the trial court. ” Washington v Washington , 283 Mich App 667, 671; 770 NW2d 908 (2009). 
We also review de novo “[w]hether an arbitrator exceeded his or her authority. ” Id. at 672. A 
court’s role in reviewing an arbitration award is limited. TSP Servs, 329 Mich App at 619. Courts 
may not review the arbitrator’s factual findings and instead review the arbitrator’s decision only 
for errors of law. Id. at 620. “Not every error of law by an arbitrator, however, merits subsequent 
court intervention.” Id. The error of law “must be so substantial that, but for the error, the award 
would have been substantially different.” Washington, 283 Mich App at 672 (quotation marks and 
citation omitted). Such an error must also “be discernible on the face of the award itself,” meaning 
“only a legal error that is evident without scrutiny of intermediate mental indicia will suffice to 
overturn an arbitration award.” Id. (quotation marks and citation omitted). In other words, courts 
will not “engage in a review of an arbitrator ’s mental process[.] ” TSP Servs, 329 Mich App at 
620. 
A trial court “shall enforce an arbitrator’s award . . . in the same manner as an order issued 
by the circuit court .” MCL 600.5079(1). Under MCL 600.5081(2), a court shall vacate an 
arbitration award when: 
 (a) The award was procured by corruption, fraud, or other undue means. 
 (b) There was evident partiality by an arbitrator appointed as a neutral, 
corruption of an arbitrator, or misconduct prejudicing a party’s rights. 
 (c) The arbitrator exceeded his or her powers. 
 (d) The arbitrator refused to postpone the hearing on a showing of sufficient 
cause, refused to hear evidence material to the controversy, or otherwise conducted 
the hearing to prejudice substantially a party’s rights. 
Arbitrators exceed their powers “whenever they act beyond the material terms of the contract from 
which they primarily draw their authority, or in contravention of controlling principles of law .” 
Washington, 283 Mich App at 672 (quotation marks and citations omitted). 
B. IMPRACTICABILITY AND IMPOSSIBILITY 
 Appellants first argue that the arbitration award must be vacated because the sprinkler 
system requirement rendered the tenants ’ performance of their obligations under the lease 
impracticable, if not impossible. The doctrine of impossibility/impracticability is a defense that 
excuses the

Filed 10/21/26 Tyron Street Acquisition Trust v. Moshe CA2/4 
NOT TO BE PUBLISHED IN THE OFFICIAL REPORTS 
California Rules of Court, rule 8.1115(a), prohibits courts and parties from citing or relying on 
opinions not certified for publication or ordered published, except as specified by rule 8.1115(a). This 
opinion has not been certified for publication or ordered published for purposes of rule 8.1115(a). 

IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA 
SECOND APPELLATE DISTRICT 
DIVISION FOUR 

TYRON STREET ACQUISITION 
TRUST I, A DELAWARE 
STATUTORY TRUST, 
 Plaintiff and Respondent, 
 v. 
YAIR BEN MOSHE, 
 Defendant and Appellant. 
B351583 
(Los Angeles County 
Super. Ct. No. 
24STCV10832) 

APPEAL from a judgment of the Superior Court of Los 
Angeles County, Gary D. Roberts, Judge. Affirmed. 
Law Offices of Jacob Reich, Jacob Reich for Defendant and 
Appellant. 
Donahue Fitzgerald, Mark D. Epstein and Garrett Burton; 
Snell & Wilmer, Andrew B. Still and Eric S. Pezold for Plaintiff 
and Respondent. 

2 

This appeal arises from cross-motions for summary 
judgment regarding lien priority over two adjacent parcels of real 
property. Tyron Street Acquisition Trust I (Tyron) contends it is 
entitled to lien priority under the doctrine of equitable 
subrogation. Yair Ben Moshe counters that equitable 
subrogation does not apply because it would elevate Tyron’s deed 
of trust to a superior position and would directly prejudice 
Moshe’s deed of trust. The trial court granted Tyron’s motion 
and denied Moshe’s, concluding that equitable subrogation 
applies in this case as a matter of law. We affirm. 
BACKGROUND 
I. Facts 
A. The Properties and the 1968 Covenant 
This case concerns lien priority over two adjacent parcels of 
real property commonly known as 1303 and 1305 Laveta Terrace 
in Los Angeles (the property). On May 29, 1968, a covenant was 
recorded against the property (the 1968 covenant). The 1968 
covenant provides that the two lots “shall be held as one parcel 
and no portion shall be sold separately.” On December 3, 2014, 
Reposition Laveta, LLC (Reposition) acquired title to both lots by 
a single grant deed. Thereafter, Reposition borrowed money 
against the property as detailed below. 
B. The Easy Financial Deeds of Trust 
On June 10, 2021, two separate deeds of trust in favor of 
Easy Financial LLC (Easy Financial) were recorded in the Los 
Angeles County’s Recorder’s Office, each encumbering one of the 

3 

two adjacent properties.1 One deed of trust secured a loan of 
$1,725,000 and encumbered the property known as 1305 Laveta 
Terrace. The other deed of trust secured a loan of $862,500 and 
encumbered the adjacent property commonly known as 1303 
Laveta Terrace. 
C. Moshe’s Deed of Trust 
On September 30, 2022, Moshe made an $800,000 loan to 
Reposition, secured by a deed of trust which encumbered both 
Laveta Terrace properties. 
D. The Churchill Loan and Payoff of the Easy 
Financial Loans 
On or about March 2, 2023, Churchill Funding LLC 
(Churchill) made a loan to Reposition in the amount of 
$2,793,750.00, secured by a deed of trust recorded on March 7, 
2023. The single deed of trust encumbered both Laveta Terrace 
properties. 
As an express condition of funding, Churchill required that 
its deed of trust record in first position and that all senior liens 
be cleared or paid through escrow. It specifically conditioned 
funding on issuance of a lender’s title policy insuring first 
priority. The preliminary report of title that Churchill received 
from Stewart Title Guaranty Company (Stewart Title) while 
underwriting the loan disclosed the Easy Financial deeds of trust, 

1 Tyron claims that on October 10, 2019, before the Easy 
Financial deeds of trust were recorded, a deed of trust in favor of 
Maxim Commercial Capital, securing a loan of $1,800,000, was 
recorded. Moshe asserts the record does not establish that the Maxim 
deed of trust remained an outstanding encumbrance when Moshe 
recorded his deed of trust. But as Moshe concedes, we need not decide 
this dispute because it has no bearing on the dispositive issues on 
appeal. 

4 

but did not disclose Moshe’s deed of trust. The lender’s title 
policy issued by Stewart Title also did not disclose Moshe’s deed 
of trust and insured Churchill’s deed of trust as first priority. 
Following the payoffs of the Easy Financial loans—
$1,777,635.28 for the first Easy Financial loan and $903,059.16 
for the second Easy Financial loan—both Easy Financial deeds of 
trust were reconveyed and released from the property of record. 
On January 26, 2024, Churchill assigned its deed of trust to 
Tyron by recorded Assignment of Security Instruments. The 
assignment included the same legal description applicable to the 
two Laveta Terrace properties. 
II. Procedural Background and the Trial Court’s 
Rulings 
On April 30, 2024, Tyron filed a complaint against Moshe 
for (1) equitable subrogation, (2) injunctive relief, (3) quiet title to 
a mortgage lien, and (4) declaratory relief. Tyron alleged that the 
purpose of the Churchill loan was to refinance and pay off the full 
balances the borrower owed on pre-existing mortgage loans that 
encumbered the property and that “both the Borrower and 
Churchill Funding, and by extension Tyron Street as the assignee 
and successor-in-interest to Churchill Funding, intended for, and 
expected that the full balance of the Loan funds would be used to 
pay off and retire the Borrower’s pre-existing secured debt on the 
Property in its entirety, and that the new Tyron Street Deed of 
Trust that secured the Loan would constitute a first priority 
position lien on the Property.” 
Tyron moved for summary adjudication of its first, third, 
and fourth causes of action. It argued that the undisputed 
evidence demonstrated the Churchill loan funds were used to 
satisfy senior encumbrances and that Churchill and Tyron 

5 

reasonably believed the loan was secured in first position. Thus, 
according to Tyron, its deed of trust—recorded after Moshe’s—
has priority under the doctrine of equitable subrogation. In 
support of its motion, Tyron submitted the declaration of 
Matthew Dameron, Director of Asset Management for Churchill 
Funding I, LLC (the master servicer and attorney-in-fact for 
Tyron), which attached the loan file records and the escrow 
disbursements paying off the Easy Financial loans. 
Moshe opposed the motion and filed evidentiary objections 
to Dameron’s declaration. Moshe argued Tyron is not entitled to 
summary adjudication because the Easy Financial loans were 
void or defective, equitable subrogation is not applicable because 
it would prejudice Moshe, there is no admissible evidence 
supporting the essential elements of equitable subrogation, and 
material issues of fact exist regarding whether Churchill had 
knowledge of Moshe’s deed of trust. 
Moshe also filed his own motion for summary judgment or, 
in the alternative, for summary adjudication on the ground that 
equitable subrogation does not apply as a matter of law because, 
according to Moshe, “granting subrogation will not just put 
[Tyron] in the shoes in which the preexisting lien holder was, 
rather it will elevate [Tyron] giving him a position far superior to 
that previously held by the prior lien holder whose debt was paid 
off and it will put [Moshe] in a position, substantially inferior to 
the position he would have been in, had the preexisting loans not 
been replaced by the Churchill Loan.” 
After a hearing, the trial court issued a 21-page written 
ruling granting Tyron’s motion and denying Moshe’s motion. The 
court concluded no material issues of fact exist as to whether 
equitable subrogation is applicable. Thus, the court granted 

6 

summary adjudication of Tyron’s claim for equitable subrogation, 
as well as Tyron’s derivative claims for quiet title and declaratory 
relief. 
The clerk then entered dismissal, at Tyron’s request, of the 
only remaining claim for injunctive relief. The trial court entered 
judgment establishing two equitable liens in favor of Tyron as 
follows: (1) Tyron’s “Deed of Trust is equitably subrogated to the 
priority position against 1305 Laveta Terrace, Los Angeles, 
California 90026 that was held by the Deed of Trust in favor of 
Easy Financial LLC recorded . . . on June 10, 2021 . . . for the 
principal amount of $1,777,635.28 plus accrued interest thereon” 
and (2) Tyron’s “Deed of Trust is equitably subrogated to the lien 
priority position against 1303 Laveta Terrace, Los Angeles, 
California 90026 that was held by the Deed of Trust in favor of 
Easy Financial LLC recorded . . . on June 10, 2021 . . . for the 
principal amount of $903,059.16 plus accrued interest thereon.” 
Moshe timely appealed. 
DISCUSSION 
I. Standard of Review 
A party is entitled to summary judgment only if there is no 
triable issue of material fact and the party is entitled to judgment 
as a matter of law. (Code Civ. Proc., § 437c, subd. (c).) A triable 
issue of fact exists if the evidence would allow a reasonable trier 
of fact to find the fact in favor of the party opposing summary 
judgment. (Aguilar v. Atlantic Richfield Co. (2001) 25 Cal.4th 
826, 850.) 
We review the trial court’s ruling on a summary judgment 
motion de novo, liberally construe the evidence in favor of the 
party opposing the motion, and resolve all doubts concerning the 
evidence in favor of the opponent. (Miller v. Department of 

7 

Corrections (2005) 36 Cal.4th 446, 460.) “We must affirm a 
summary judgment if it is correct on any of the grounds asserted 
in the trial court, regardless of the trial court’s stated reasons.” 
(Grebing v. 24 Hour Fitness USA, Inc. (2015) 234 Cal.App.4th 
631, 636—637.) 
We generally review a trial court’s ruling on evidentiary 
objections for an abuse of discretion. As to evidentiary rulings 
made in connection with a motion for summary judgment, 
however, there is a split of authority. Some courts have held 
such evidentiary rulings are reviewed for abuse of discretion 
(Martin v. Trustees of California State University (2023) 97 
Cal.App.5th 149, 161; Butte Fire Cases (2018) 24 Cal.App.5th 
1150, 1169), while other courts have held that some or all written 
objections should be reviewed de novo (Pipitone v. Williams 
(2016) 244 Cal.App.4th 1437, 1450—1451; Strobel v. Johnson & 
Johnson (2021) 70 Cal.App.5th 796, 816—817.) “We will follow 
the weight of authority and apply the abuse of discretion 
standard.” (Schmidt v. Citibank, N.A. (2018) 28 Cal.App.5th 
1109, 1118.) 
II. The Trial Court Did Not Err by Applying the 
Doctrine of Equitable Subrogation 
California law generally follows the “first in time, first in 
right” system of lien priorities. (See Civ. Code, § 2897 [“Other 
things being equal, different liens upon the same property have 
priority according to the time of their creation”].) However, the 
“doctrine of equitable subrogation is an exception to the first in 
time, first in right rule and applies in those situations where 
equity requires a different result.” (JP Morgan Chase Bank, N.A. 
v. Banc of America Practice Solutions, Inc. (2012) 209 
Cal.App.4th 855, 860 (Chase).) 

8 

Nearly a century ago, our Supreme Court stated the 
general rule applicable to a lender’s entitlement to equitable 
subrogation: “ ‘One who advances money to pay off an 
encumbrance on realty at the instance of either the owner of the 
property or the holder of the incumbrance, either on the express 
understanding, or under circumstances from which an 
understanding will be implied, that the advance made is to be 
secured by a first lien on the property, is not a mere volunteer; 
and in the event the new security is for any reason not a first lien 
on the property, the holder of such security, if not chargeable 
with culpable and inexcusable neglect, will be subrogated to the 
rights of the prior encumbrancer under the security held by him, 
unless the superior or equal equi

leads.caseName: Dworman v. PHH Mortgage Services
leads.court: Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
leads.text:
United States Court of Appeals 
For the First Circuit 

No. 25-1407 
ALAN DWORMAN, 
Plaintiff, Appellant, 
v. 
PHH MORTGAGE SERVICES; OCWEN LOAN SERVICING, LLC, 

Defendants, Appellees, 
FIRST OHIO BANC & LENDING, INC., 

Defendant. 

APPEAL FROM THE UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT 
FOR THE DISTRICT OF MASSACHUSETTS 

[Hon. Margaret R. Guzman, U.S. District Judge] 

Before 

Barron, Chief Judge, 
Gelpí and Aframe, Circuit Judges. 

 J. Mark Dickison , with whom Brendan P. Slean and Lawson & 
Weitzen, LLP were on brief, for appellant. 

 Marissa I. Delinks, with whom Maura K. McKelvey and Hinshaw 
& Culbertson LLP were on brief, for appellees. 

October 21, 2026 

- 2 - 
AFRAME, Circuit Judge . After defaulting on a home 
mortgage loan, Alan Dworman agreed with his loan servicer that if 
he met certain repayment conditions, a portion of his loan balance 
would be forgiven. Dworman failed to meet those conditions. He 
nonetheless claimed that the loan servicer and its successor had 
forgiven his debt by issuing him an Internal Revenue Service 
("IRS") Form 1099-C, entitled "Cancellation of Debt," and through 
certain other conduct related to the debt's collection . They 
disagreed. 
With his debt unforgiven, Dworman sued his loan servicer 
and its successor in state court, asserting claims for breach of 
contract, breach of the covenant of good faith and fair dealing, 
and violation of the Massachusetts consumer protection statute , 
Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 93A ("Chapter 93A") , as well as seeking 
declaratory relief . Based on diversity jurisdiction, the 
defendants removed the case to federal court. In due course, the 
defendants moved for summary judgment on all claims. The district 
court rejected Dworman's contention that it would be premature to 
rule on the summary judgment motion without permitting additional 
discovery and then granted the motion. Dworman appeals from the 
denial of his request for additional discovery and the grant of 
summary judgment. We affirm in both respects. 
- 3 - 
I. 
A. 
In 2007, Dworman obtained a $549,600 mortgage loan from 
First Ohio Banc & Lending, Inc. ("First Ohio Banc") to refinance 
an existing mortgage on his Massachusetts residence. The following 
year, Dworman lost his job and fell behind on paying his mortgage. 
In early 2016, Dworman sought mortgage assistance from Ocwen Loan 
Servicing, LLC ("Ocwen"), his loan servicer at the time. Ocwen 
offered Dworman a "Home Affordable Loan Modification Trial Period 
Plan," which Dworman accepted in July 2016. Under the plan, after 
successfully making three reduced monthly payments, Dworman became 
eligible for a permanent loan modification agreement. In November 
2016, Dworman entered into such an agreement with Ocwen (the "2016 
Agreement"). The U.S. Department of Treasury paid Ocwen a $1,200 
incentive for implementing the 2016 Agreement. 
Per the 2016 A greement, Dworman's delinquent taxes, 
insurance, and interest were capitalized into a new principal 
balance of $821,864.94. Section 3(c) of the 2016 Agreement 
provided that $465,114.94 of this balance would be deferred (the 
"Deferred Principal Balance") and that Dworman would not pay 
interest or make monthly payments on the Deferred Principal Balance 
until the loan's maturity date. It further stated that $406,714.94 
of the Deferred Principal Balance (the "Deferred Principal 
Reduction Amount") was "eligible for forgiveness." So long as 
- 4 - 
Dworman was "not in default on [his] new payments such that the 
equivalent of three full monthly payments are due and unpaid on 
the last day of any month," one third of the Deferred Principal 
Reduction Amount would be forgiven on each of the first, second, 
and third anniversaries of September 1, 2016. 
On December 5, 2016, four days after the 2016 Agreement 
became effective, Ocwen sent Dworman an IRS Form 1099-C, entitled 
"Cancellation of Debt," which listed $406,714.94 as the "[a]mount 
of debt discharged." The Form 1099-C notifies the IRS of the 
discharged amount because it may be considered income for federal 
tax purposes. Dworman filed the Form 1099 -C with his 2016 tax 
return, reporting the Deferred Principal Reduction Amount as 
income. 
Dworman missed his first modified mortgage payment and 
continued to fall behind on payments. Throughout 2017, Ocwen sent 
Dworman numerous communications indicating his arrearages. And in 
May of that year, Ocwen assisted Dworman in trying to bring his 
account current by sending him a temporary repayment agreement. 
Dworman's default status continued into 2018, and Ocwen 
issued further delinquency notices. In mid -March 2018, for 
example, Ocwen sent Dworman a notice advising that his loan had 
been referred to counsel to begin foreclosure proceedings and 
included a notice of debt indicating that "[t]he amount of debt as 
of March 12, 2018 is $832,109.93." Later that month, Dworman 
- 5 - 
entered into a repayment agreement with Ocwen, but he nonetheless 
remained delinquent. In September 2018, Ocwen sent a mortgage 
statement reflecting that the loan was 169 days delinquent and 
that Dworman's total principal balance was $813,995.09, comprising 
a regular principal balance of $348,880.15 and a Deferred Principal 
Balance of $465,114.94. Ocwen sent Dworman similar mortgage 
statements in February and April 2019; each noted Dworman's 
delinquency and listed the Deferred Principal Balance as 
$465,114.94. 
On June 4, 2019, PHH Mortgage Corporation ("PHH") sent 
Dworman a notice informing him that it had merged with Ocwen and 
that PHH was now servicing his loan (the "June 2019 Transfer 
Notice"). Dworman acknowledge d receiving this Notice, which 
included an addendum indicating that the principal balance for 
Dworman's account as of June 1, 2019, was $342,838.62. The June 
2019 Transfer Notice did not , however, mention the Deferred 
Principal Balance. On August 13, 2019, PHH sent Dworman a letter 
amending the Notice, stating that it had omitted the Deferred 
Principal Balance and clarifying that "[t]he correct principal 
balance as of [June 1, 2019] which includes the deferred principal 
balance was: $807,953.56. " Dworman denies having received this 
letter, although it was sent to the same address as the June 2019 
Transfer Notice. 
- 6 - 
On April 6, 2020, in response to Dworman's request for 
a payoff letter on his loan, PHH notified Dworman that the Deferred 
Principal Balance "was not forgiven," as Dworman had been 
delinquent in his loan payments on the first anniversary of the 
2016 Agreement. Dworman admit ted that he received this 
notification. In 2020, Dworman caught up on his loan obligations 
and has since made timely payments. 
Dworman filed suit in January 2023, naming First Ohio 
Banc, Ocwen, and PHH as defendants.1 The parties then engaged in 
discovery, during which Dworman directed document requests to 
Ocwen. Relevant here, Dworman sought documents from Ocwen 
"relating to any tax write offs, financial benefits and incentives 
extended to Ocwen . . . including but not limited to Ocwen's tax 
filings 2016 to present." In Dworman's vie w, these documents 
pertained to whether Ocwen had received the benefit of a tax 
write-off for issuing the Form 1099-C, which would tend to suggest 
that it treated the Deferred Principal Reduction Amount as 
discharged. By that time, the mortgagee and note holder had moved 
from First Ohio Banc to Deutsche Bank National Trust Company as 
Trustee for IndyMac INDX Mortgage Loan Trust 2007 -AR17, Mortgage 
Pass-Through Certificates Series 2007 -AR17 ( "Deutsche Bank 
Trust"). Deutsche Bank Trust was not named in these requests, nor 

1 Following the appeal, Dworman voluntarily dismissed his 
claims against First Ohio Banc, the original mortgagee. 
- 7 - 
was it ever named a party to Dworman's suit. Ocwen objected to 
Dworman's request for its tax filings on relevance grounds and did 
not produce them during the litigation. 
B. 
Following discovery, Ocwen and PHH (collectively, "the 
defendants") moved for summary judgment on all claims. Dworman 
opposed the motion, both on the merits and because it was premature 
insofar as he needed further discovery into Ocwen's 2016 tax 
filings.2 On the latter argument, the district court determined 
that Ocwen's refusal to produce its 2016 tax filings posed no 
impediment to resolving the summary judgment motion because 
Dworman had failed to explain why Ocwen's tax filings were material 
to his summary judgment opposition. 
On the merits, for Dworman's breach of contract claim, 
the district court concluded that the undisputed factual record 
demonstrated that the defendants did not breach the 2016 Agreement 
by failing to forgive the Deferred Principal Reduction Amount. In 
support, the court pointed to undisputed evidence that Dworman 
failed to meet the contractual conditions for loan forgiveness in 
Section 3(c) of the Agreement -- i.e., not falling more than three 
months behind on payments. The court also rejected Dworman's 

2 Dworman first raised this discovery issue at the summary 
judgment stage by filing a Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 56(d) 
affidavit with his opposition to the defendants' summary judgment 
motion. 
- 8 - 
argument that the defendants had waived their right to claim that 
he breached the 2016 Agreement by accepting his late mortgage 
payments. The court concluded that Section 12 of the 2016 
Agreement expressly provided that Ocwen's acceptance of late 
payments would not waive any right or remedy. 
Additionally, the district court dispensed with 
Dworman's argument that issuance of the Form 1099 -C and the 
defendants' subsequent conduct operated to discharge his debt. In 
so doing, the court cited the "majority view" that issuing a Form 
1099-C does not legally discharge a debt but rather satisfies an 
IRS reporting requirement. Likewise, the court rejected Dworman's 
claim that PHH's omission of the Deferred Principal Reduction 
Amount from the June 2019 Transfer Notice reflected forgiveness of 
that amount. The court reasoned that PHH's failure to mention the 
Deferred Principal Reduction Amount did not constitute express 
forgiveness, and it found that PHH's August 13, 2019, corrective 
letter timely accounted for the Deferred Principal Balance. 
For Dworman's claim alleging breach of the covenant of 
good faith and fair dealing, the district court determined that no 
reasonable jury could find the requisite "dishonest purpose or 
conscious wrongdoing" by the defendants. Quoting Conte v. Bank of 
Am., N.A., 52 F. Supp. 3d 265, 269 (D. Mass. 2014). To the 
contrary, the defendants attemp ted to provide Dworman with 
multiple debt relief options, engaged in good-faith conduct by 
- 9 - 
entering the 2016 Agreement, and applied the contract terms as 
written. 
Next, the district court concluded that Dworman's 
Chapter 93A claim failed for procedural and substantive reasons. 
Procedurally, Dworman's complaint failed to allege that he sent 
the required pre-suit demand letter to the defendants . 
Substantively, the court concluded that the Chapter 93A claim 
failed because it was predicated on the same insufficient breach 
arguments underlying Dworman's other claims. And even if the 
defendants had breached the 2016 Agreement , the record did not 
show the kind of egregiously wrong conduct contemplated by Chapter 
93A. 
Finally, the district court rejected Dworman's 
derivative declaratory judgment claim, reasoning that there was no 
justification to issue a declaration that the Deferred Principal 
Reduction Amount had been forgiven given the failure of his other 
claims. 
Dworman timely appealed. 
II. 
A. 
We review de novo the district court's grant 
of summary judgment. Henderson v. Mass. Bay Transp. Auth., 977 
F.3d 20, 29 (1st Cir. 2020). In conducting our review, we construe 
the facts and all reasonable inferences from those facts in favor 
- 10 - 
of the non -movant -- here, Dworman. See Pleasantdale Condos. , 
L

leads.caseName: U.S. Bank N.A. v. Pursoo
leads.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York
leads.text:
U.S. Bank N.A. v Pursoo 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06161 
 October 21, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 U.S. Bank National Association, etc., appellant, 
 v 
 Leon Pursoo, respondent, et al., defendants. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on October 21, 2026 
 2025-02144, (Index No. 12192/09) 
 Mark C. Dillon, J.P. 
 Valerie Brathwaite Nelson 
 Laurence L. Love 
 James P. McCormack, JJ. 

 Hinshaw & Culbertson LLP, New York, NY (Ali Degan and Schuyler B. Kraus of counsel), for appellant. 
 Yolande I. Nicholson, P.C., Brooklyn, NY, for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action to foreclose a mortgage, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Nassau County (Danielle M. Peterson, J.), entered January 30, 2025. The order, insofar as appealed from, denied the plaintiff's motion, inter alia, for a judgment of foreclosure and sale, granted that branch of the cross-motion of the defendant Leon Pursoo which was pursuant to CPLR 5015 to vacate an order of the same court dated July 27, 2022, granting the plaintiff's motion, among other things, for an order of reference and for leave to enter a default judgment against that defendant and, upon vacatur, pursuant to CPLR 306-b and 3211(a)(8) to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against him, and denied the plaintiff's cross-motion pursuant to CPLR 306-b to extend the time to serve the summons and complaint upon the defendant Leon Pursoo. 
 ORDERED that the order entered January 30, 2025, is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs. 
 In December 2009, the plaintiff's predecessor in interest, GMC Mortgage, LLC, commenced this action against, among others, the defendant Leon Pursoo (hereinafter the defendant) to foreclosure a mortgage encumbering certain real property located in Westbury. The plaintiff failed to serve the defendant within 120 days of the commencement of the action. In February 2011, the plaintiff voluntarily discontinued the action. In October 2017, the plaintiff moved to vacate the voluntary discontinuance and restore the action to the active calendar, and, in an order entered April 30, 2018, the Supreme Court granted the motion. 
 On December 9, 2019, 10 years after the commencement of this action and more than 1 year after it was restored to the active calendar, the plaintiff purportedly served the defendant with the summons and complaint. In February 2020, the plaintiff moved, inter alia, for an order of reference and for leave to enter a default judgment against the defendant. In an order dated July 27, 2022 (hereinafter the July 2022 order), the Supreme Court granted the motion. In January 2024, the plaintiff moved, among other things, for a judgment of foreclosure and sale. The defendant cross-moved, inter alia, pursuant to CPLR 5015 to vacate the July 2022 order and, upon vacatur, pursuant to CPLR 306-b and 3211(a)(8) to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against him. Thereafter, the plaintiff cross-moved pursuant to CPLR 306-b to extend the time to serve the summons and complaint upon the defendant. In an order entered January 30, 2025, the court, among other things, [*2] denied the plaintiff's motion, granted that branch of the defendant's cross-motion, and denied the plaintiff's cross-motion. The plaintiff appeals. 
 Generally, service of a summons and complaint must be made within 120 days after the commencement of the action ( see CPLR 306-b). Whether to grant "[a]n extension of time" to effectuate "service is a matter within the court's discretion" ( Leader v Maroney, Ponzini & Spencer , 97 NY2d 95, 101). "Pursuant to CPLR 306-b, a court may, in the exercise of its discretion, grant a motion for an extension of time within which to effect service of the summons and complaint for good cause shown or in the interest of justice" ( Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Gewirtz , 204 AD3d 1070, 1072; see Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Martinez , 211 AD3d 909, 911). "Good cause and interest of justice are two separate and independent statutory standards" ( Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Fameux , 201 AD3d 1012, 1013). Good cause requires a showing of reasonable diligence in attempting to effect service ( see Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Gewirtz , 204 AD3d at 1072; Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Fameux , 201 AD3d at 1014). In deciding whether to grant a motion to extend the time for service in the interest of justice, the court must carefully analyze "the factual setting of the case and . . . balanc[e] . . . the competing interests presented by the parties. Unlike an extension request premised on good cause, a plaintiff need not establish reasonably diligent efforts at service as a threshold matter" ( Leader v Maroney, Ponzini & Spencer , 97 NY2d at 105). "Under the interest of justice standard, 'the court may consider diligence, or lack thereof, along with any other relevant factor in making its determination, including expiration of the Statute of Limitations, the meritorious nature of the cause of action, the length of delay in service, the promptness of a plaintiff's request for the extension of time, and prejudice to defendant'" ( Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Gewirtz , 204 AD3d at 1072, quoting Leader v Maroney, Ponzini & Spencer , 97 NY2d at 105-106). 
 Here, the plaintiff did not contend that it attempted to serve the defendant within 120 days of the commencement of this action and, therefore, failed to show good cause for an extension of time to serve the summons and complaint upon the defendant ( see Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Fameux , 201 AD3d at 1014). Additionally, the plaintiff failed to establish that an extension of time was warranted in the interest of justice. The plaintiff failed to offer any excuse for its delay of approximately 15 years from the commencement of this action to move to extend the time to serve the summons and complaint upon the defendant. Moreover, the plaintiff submitted no evidence that the defendant had actual notice of the action within 120 days of its commencement ( see id. ; Federal Natl. Mtge. Assn. v Cassis , 187 AD3d 1145, 1147). Accordingly, the court properly denied the plaintiff's cross-motion pursuant to CPLR 306-b to extend the time to serve the summons and complaint upon the defendant. 
 Since the defendant was not properly served with the summons and complaint and the plaintiff failed to demonstrate entitlement to an extension of time to effectuate service, the Supreme Court properly granted that branch of the defendant's cross-motion which was pursuant to CPLR 5015 to vacate the July 2022 order and, upon vacatur, pursuant to CPLR 306-b and 3211(a)(8) to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against him ( see HSBC Bank USA, N.A. v Labin , 232 AD3d 861, 865; see Citimortgage, Inc. v Unger , 230 AD3d 1226, 1227) and denied the plaintiff's motion for a judgment of foreclosure and sale. 
 DILLON, J.P., BRATHWAITE NELSON, LOVE and MCCORMACK, JJ., concur.
